1	# Evaluating and routing a new item
2	
3	The shared method for three decisions every proposed addition to this corpus must pass through: **is it worthy** of inclusion at all, **which mechanism** should carry it, and — only for prose — **where does it go**. Any routine or person that adds an item — the [growth promote stage](tasks/growth-promote/task.md), an owner-requested retrospective pass, a hand edit — applies this same protocol, so the decision-making lives here once instead of being re-derived per caller.
4	
5	This is a Claudinite-internal doc used by the growth lifecycle (see [the canon-curation README](README.md)): it is **not** part of the mounted corpus and consuming repos do not `@import` it.
6	
7	An "item" is one **distilled, portable rule** — not a transcript, not a narration of what happened. A candidate still phrased as "here's what we did" has not been distilled yet and is below the bar on form alone, before any of the tests below. This doc picks up once a distilled rule exists and decides its fate.
8	
9	## Worthiness — does it earn a place at all
10	
11	The corpus is read read-only by every consuming repo, so a **duplicative** item (already covered) or an **undistilled** one (a story or a truism, not a rule) pollutes shared canon and costs every future reader. The bar guards against *those* — it is **not** a bar on *scope*: an item useful to only one project today can still earn a place (see Portable). Admit an item only when **all** hold:
12	
13	- **Distilled.** It is a single tight rule in the imperative, not a story, a log, or a restatement of a generic truism.
14	- **Portable — would a *future* project benefit?** Not "useful to every project today." An item can help only **one** project right now and still belong here, so long as another project — **especially one with a similar tech stack or process** — would benefit when it arrives. Being specific to a technology or a process is **not** disqualifying: generalize it and route it to that technology's or practice's home. What disqualifies is leaning on *this* project's non-transferable particulars — a product requirement, or a one-off incident in how it happened to call some API. The test, a genuinely hard one: *if another project with a similar tech stack came along, would it benefit from this?* Yes → portable; only-ever-this-product → local. A rule mined from Claudinite's own test suite is the hardest case: it reads as generic testing craft even when it actually depends on Claudinite's own shape — the only project whose tests build git-repo fixtures because its checks take a repo as input. Before promoting one, grep the fleet's own callers of the pattern the rule is about; zero callers outside this project's own conformance tests means the lesson is local however general its wording (#857: a fixture-signing rule read as portable, was promoted to `writing-tests`, then reverted once every caller of the fixture helper turned out to be a Claudinite conformance test).
15	- **Durable and reusable.** It will still apply on a future, unseen task — not a one-off, not a situational detail, not something already implied by an existing rule.
16	- **Readable through the channel it lands in.** A rule whose premise is that the delivery channel
17	  itself failed cannot be carried by that channel. Promote #497 admitted "the tell that the SessionStart
18	  hook did not fire" as pack prose — and pack prose is what that hook delivers, so in the one situation
19	  the rule describes it is not in context to be read. Detecting a channel's own failure belongs in code,
20	  not in the payload the channel carries; reject such an item here rather than rewording it.
21	- **Not already covered.** The insight does not already exist **anywhere** in the corpus, even worded differently or owned by a different file. This is checked against the *entire* corpus, not just the file it would land in — see [Dedupe against the whole corpus](#dedupe-against-the-whole-corpus).
22	
23	Reject on any miss — but the misses that matter are *undistilled*, *already-covered*, or *genuinely one-off*, not merely *narrow*. When you're torn over a real, non-duplicate rule, lean toward **keeping** it — the goal is a broad library. When you're torn over whether something is a duplicate, or a rule at all, leave it out. The failure to avoid is padding the canon with restatements of what's already there; admitting a narrow-but-reusable rule is not that failure.
24	
25	### Dedupe against the whole corpus
26	
27	Before admitting anything, read across the corpus, not only the file you expect to own the item. The same insight is frequently already present under a different heading or in an adjacent group. If it sharpens an **existing** rule, fold it in with a minimal edit rather than adding a second bullet that says nearly the same thing — and never weaken or restate what is already there in the process.
28	
29	**Sweep last, and case-insensitively.** A dedupe pass is only evidence about the text it actually read, so it runs **after** every re-home, merge and edit the change makes — a sweep run early and never re-run reports clean on content that has since moved under it. Measured on #740 (the seven-PR promote consolidation): the sweep ran *before* two lessons were re-homed out of a folded-away skill file into `packs/basics/RULES.md`, and **three** copies of the same unknown-state rule reached the owner, who found them by reading. The re-run then surfaced a further pair the pattern had missed because it was case-sensitive and the survivors were capitalised. So: sweep as the last step, match case-insensitively, and state the similarity threshold you swept at so the "no remaining near-duplicates" claim is checkable.
30	
31	## Mechanism triage — prose is the fallback, not the default
32	
33	A worthy item next descends the **promotion ladder** ([../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md) owns it): platform setting (always paired with its verifying check) → PreToolUse hook → conformance check → skill → prose. The *first* rung that can carry the item wins — a rule about repo state becomes a check whose failure message *is* the lesson; a bad action to prevent becomes a guard; a procedure or knowledge with a nameable trigger becomes (or joins) a skill. Only an item none of those can carry — judgment, in-flight behavior, signature-less knowledge — proceeds to the file routing below, and its landing **names that reason** in the promote log so conversion rates stay auditable.
34	
35	**"No universal signature" alone never routes an item to prose.** A rule converts to a check when a *narrow, file-scoped* signature covers the **grounded cases** — the concrete shapes the rule was distilled from — even though no signature covers every conceivable violation. Gate it relevance-first so it stays inert off-target, and document the genuinely signature-less residue in the rule's own comments as out of scope. The prose rung is only for an item whose grounded cases *themselves* have no reliable signature (pure judgment, runtime/in-flight behavior).
36	
37	## Routing — picking the right file (rung-5 items only)
38	
39	Routing is robust when it keys on **stable file groups**, not on the current roster of individual files (which grows over time). The corpus is organized into a few groups, each with its own selection rule:
40	
41	1. **The practice group** — durable, project-agnostic practices, each file a self-contained, reusable unit of know-how the agent applies whenever its subject comes up (engineering, agentic, git/GitHub, testing, investigation, discipline, architecture), partitioned **by kind of practice** with each file owning one recurring subject cluster. This group spans **two folders that differ only by *when* the rule loads**: `always/` for a rule that applies to essentially every task (the index `@`-imports it, so it's force-loaded every session), and `tasks/` for a subject-gated rule read on demand when its trigger fires. Route in two steps: first match the item's *kind* to the file whose cluster already owns that subject; then keep it in `always/` only if it genuinely isn't tied to one kind of task (the rare case — `always/` stays small), otherwise it belongs in `tasks/`. Read the group's own index (the root `CLAUDE.md`) to find the current owner for a kind — never from memory, since the set of clusters can grow.
42	2. **The per-user group** — interaction preferences and trigger phrases. This group does **not live in this repo**: an item of this kind routes out to the person it belongs to, never into the practice group and never back into the canon.
43	3. **The per-technology group** — practices specific to one technology, **one file per technology**. Route a technology-specific item to that technology's file. When **no pack homes that technology** (not even a stub), the item doesn't land in a loose doc — it **mints a fingerprinted stub pack** (a `packs/<tech>/`, delivered in its own PR), so the next project on that stack self-declares it; [promote](tasks/growth-promote/task.md)'s stub-minting floor and [the generate-project-instructions skill](../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/skills/generate-project-instructions/SKILL.md) own the mechanics.
44	
45	Pick **exactly one** owner. If an item plausibly fits two files, choose the single best one — never split one item across files, and never duplicate it into both. The group decides the *axis* (kind, person, or technology); the file within the group is then the one whose existing scope the item falls squarely inside.
46	
47	### When nothing fits
48	
49	An item that matches **no** existing file is **not** a reject signal by itself — a genuinely new category of lesson is meant to be learnable, so a worthy item that no file owns earns its own file. Resolve it in this order:
50	
51	- **Route into an existing owner** when one genuinely fits — the first choice. If the item belongs to a file's cluster and merely sits slightly off-center, a small stretch toward that owner beats spinning up a new file. A new file is for when no existing file's scope genuinely fits, **not** a way to dodge folding into an existing owner.
52	- **Open a new file** when the item clears the [Worthiness](#worthiness--does-it-earn-a-place-at-all) bar in full — distilled, portable, durable and reusable, and not already covered anywhere in the corpus — **and** no existing file's scope genuinely fits it. That is the whole bar: nothing more is required. Do **not** also demand that you expect the cluster to recur, that forcing the item into the closest file would *distort* it, or default to rejecting when the new-file call is a close one — those extra hurdles are dropped. Creating a file obliges registering it where the corpus is indexed and in any routing table, in the **same** change, so it never lands orphaned (see [Keep the write surface bounded](#keep-the-write-surface-bounded)).
53	
54	The loosening above is **only** to the new-cluster hurdle, never to the per-item bar. An item that misses [Worthiness](#worthiness--does-it-earn-a-place-at-all) — a one-off, non-portable or project-specific, a restatement of a generic truism, or already covered anywhere in the corpus — is rejected whether or not a file already exists for it; for the per-item admission decision, the default-to-reject-when-unsure tiebreak still stands.
55	
56	## Keep the write surface bounded
57	
58	Once worthiness and routing are settled, the edit touches **only** the single owning file: add or sharpen one terse rule in that file's existing voice and format, and change nothing else. Do not "improve" unrelated rules while you are in there. The sole exception is the new-file path above, whose surface is itself bounded to the new file plus its index and routing-table registration.
59

1	# Growth — promote lessons into the canon (the central stage)
2	
3	The [growth lifecycle](../../README.md)'s central stage: read the target members' local packs, lift the portable lessons into the shared canon, and open a PR against the canon's default branch **for the owner to approve**. Declared only by the Claudinite home repo, so it runs **once, centrally**, never per project.
4	
5	The run's **Context section is binding scope**: it names the exact target members (those whose local packs changed in the window). Work exactly that list — the fleet enumeration already happened in the precondition; **do not enumerate the fleet yourself or widen past the Context**.
6	
7	Promotion is the **judgment gate before shared canon**. This run opens a PR and **never arms auto-merge** — the owner approves it. But don't lean on that review as the portability check: [extract](../../../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/tasks/growth-extract/task.md) stays project-specific by design, so it's no second opinion, and the owner can't re-derive every portability call. This task's judgment is the real thing between a bad rule and every project that reads the canon — keep the bar high (dedupe against the whole corpus; default to reject when unsure).
8	
9	## Conventions used in this doc
10	
11	- **GitHub access is MCP-only** (`mcp__github__*`). You are outside each member repo — read its files over the API (get-file-contents, never a cross-repo checkout; the sandbox has no cross-repo git). The canon PR is opened over MCP too.
12	- **A member's local packs** are everything under `.claudinite/local/packs/` (the legacy `.claudinite/local_packs/` accepted during the rename window) — its own packs, never the read-only mounted canon elsewhere under `.claudinite/`.
13	- **`main`** stands for the canon's default branch.
14	
15	## What each run does
16	
17	### 1. Read the target members' local **packs**
18	
19	For each member named in Context, read its **local packs**. The candidate pool is a local pack's captured knowledge — its `RULES.md` **prose** AND its own **checks** (a `<pack>/*.mjs` rule module — its id, description, and failure message *are* a captured, enforceable lesson; the strongest promotion lifts it to a **canon check**, generalized, reusing the [prose-to-checks](../../../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/skills/prose-to-checks/SKILL.md) mechanics — or to canon prose when it doesn't generalize to a check). **Out of scope, staying put:** a lesson deliberately placed as a **code comment at its call site**, a project's task scripts, product source, and config. Never promote from product source. A genuinely portable rule that looks trapped in a code comment was mis-placed at extract time — leave it for a future extract pass to re-home into a pack. You don't need to tell new from old — the dedup step drops anything the canon already carries. No barrier holds tonight's extracts: read whatever is already **merged** on each member's default branch; anything landing mid-run is tomorrow's input.
20	
21	### 2. Generalize each candidate — *before* judging whether it belongs
22	
23	Generalize first, then decide worthiness — never the reverse. The act of generalizing is itself the portability probe — a rule that goes vacuous when lifted, or only makes sense with its project's context, isn't portable; leave it local. Work the rule standalone (origin naming and grouping carry no weight); strip the project (names, files, example stay in the origin repo — promote the distilled rule only); a **technology** mention isn't a disqualifier (lift it to the broadest scope that stays true — tech-specific is fine, *product*-specific is not); decide tool-vs-process and frame it for that home.
24	
25	### 3. Then judge worthiness — deduped against the *entire* corpus
26	
27	Holding the generalized rule, decide if it earns a place by the bar [item-routing.md](../../item-routing.md) owns (don't restate its gates). Lean **inclusive** — keep anything a future project could use — but be strict about **duplication**: dedupe against **every** corpus doc, not only the one you'd expect to own it.
28	
29	### 4. Triage the mechanism, then route
30	
31	- **Descend the promotion ladder first** ([item-routing.md](../../item-routing.md)'s mechanism triage). Prose is the fallback, not the default: a lesson a check can carry is **authored as the check** in this PR — the rule module in the right pack, the failure message carrying the generalized lesson, **plus a fixture test proving it fires** on a violating input and stays quiet on a clean one. When a confident detection-plus-fixture can't be authored unattended, land the lesson as prose **and** open a tagged conformance-backlog issue — never a silently-shipped broken check.
32	- **Route** each prose rule to its **one** owning doc ([item-routing.md](../../item-routing.md) owns the placement); match its voice and format; pick exactly one owner, never split or duplicate.
33	- **A technology with no home → mint a fingerprinted stub pack, in its own PR**, reusing the pack-writing mechanics [the generate-project-instructions skill](../../../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/skills/generate-project-instructions/SKILL.md) owns — `packs/<tech>/` with `pack.mjs` (add the `marker`/`detect` fingerprint when the technology carries a reliable one, else `detect: null`), a `RULES.md` seeded from the lesson, a `README.md`, and its `packs/README.md` index row. A minted pack ships in its **own** PR, split from the run's lesson-promotion PR (a new pack earns its own review surface). Never mint from imagination and never park an empty one to fill later — a pack minted here is populated from the *real, portable lesson* that justified it. Do not pad it with speculative rules no project earned — the "written from imagination, not distilled from worked examples" failure; an ungroundable rule isn't written. (Authoring a *fuller* pack from a technology's usage across the whole fleet — rather than a single lesson — is the per-repo pack-discovery task's job, not this floor's.) The follow-ups a fresh stub invites — enriching it from known best practices, triaging which skills it should require, spinning up dependent/aspect packs — are **not** automated here: note them for the owner and leave them to a later, deliberate pass.
34	- **Write it terse — when + what.** State the relevance (*when* it applies) and the rule (*what* to do); add a *why* only to flag severity, in a few words.
35	- **Bounded write surface — `packs/`/`skills/` only** (CI-enforced on the PR). Edit only the one owning doc — or, for a check-conversion, only the new rule module, its registration in the pack registry, and its fixture test. Don't "improve" unrelated rules while you're in there. The two bounded exceptions (both within `packs/`): the new-doc path [item-routing.md](../../item-routing.md) owns, and minting a stub pack.
36	- **Bump the `version` of every pack you edited** (`packs/<id>/pack.mjs`) — a pack's directory reaches a member only when that number exceeds the one the member has installed, so a promoted lesson left at the old version stays in the canon. The run's own Stop sweep reds on a pack edit that leaves the number alone.
37	- **Open a PR against `main`** on a per-run-unique branch — one PR for the whole run's accepted lessons (a minted stub is the exception: its own PR). Never a direct push. Keep every commit and PR terse. **Put the issue reference in the commit message** (`Refs #<n>` for the tracker below) — the `basics` `task-lifecycle` check reds CI on a promote commit that cites none.
38	
39	### 5. Log the run to the tracker
40	
41	Append a dated comment for every run that promoted at least one lesson, and for any notable rejection.
42	
43	## Tracking issue
44	
45	The standing self-improvement log is the issue titled exactly **`Claudinite tracker: Promote to Canon`**.
46	
47	- **Find it by that exact title, never a fuzzy match or a hard-coded number** (a bare number can dangle).
48	- **Create it already closed if missing** — creation always lands an issue open and ignores a `state: closed` argument, so create it and close it in a second call. **Never open, close, or reopen it** afterward — its state carries no meaning; only the log does.
49	- Log each run as a **dated comment** — not a sub-issue, so history accumulates in one scrollable feed — the date, and per lesson: the origin repo, the **ladder rung it landed on** (check id / skill / owning doc, with the named reason when prose was the fallback), and the generalized rule (or, for a notable rejection, the reason and the existing rule that already covers it).
50	
51	## What this task must never do
52	
53	- **Never mine outside a local pack** — product source, task scripts, code comments, and config are out of scope; only a local pack's `RULES.md` prose and its own check modules are candidates.
54	- **Never promote a product-specific or one-off item** — it stays in that project's local packs.
55	- **Never weaken, restate, or duplicate an existing rule** — fold a genuine sharpening in per [item-routing.md](../../item-routing.md) instead.
56	- **Never widen past the Context member list**, and **never touch a member repo** — this task only reads members and writes the canon PR.
57	- **Every step is a judgment call** (portability, duplication, ownership, how to generalize without distorting), and a plausible-but-wrong *acceptance* is what the owner's review is least likely to catch.
58

1	# Web Speech APIs
2	
3	Portable, project-agnostic practices for browser voice I/O — speech-to-text
4	(`webkitSpeechRecognition` / the Web Speech `SpeechRecognition` API) and
5	text-to-speech (`chrome.tts` / `speechSynthesis`) — true for any app that reads
6	or listens through the browser, read cold. These are runtime browser-behaviour
7	gotchas, knowledge you carry into the code rather than state a tool can read off
8	the repo.
9	
10	> Some of these APIs (`chrome.tts`) are extension-only; where a rule touches
11	> MV3 service-worker / content-script mechanics, only the speech-API facet is
12	> here — the general extension gotcha underneath is not.
13	
14	## Speech-to-text (`webkitSpeechRecognition` / Web Speech API)
15	
16	- **The recognizer owns its own microphone capture — you cannot hand it
17	  `getUserMedia` audio constraints.** `echoCancellation` / `noiseSuppression` /
18	  `autoGainControl` are `getUserMedia` *microphone* constraints, and the recognizer
19	  exposes no hook to set them on its internal stream (Chrome applies its default
20	  echo cancellation there regardless). To *warm* the device with a known processing
21	  state — and to read back whether echo cancellation actually engaged — run a
22	  separate preflight `getUserMedia({ audio: {…} })` capture and stop its tracks.
23	  (`suppressLocalAudioPlayback` /
24	  `restrictOwnAudio` are `getDisplayMedia` *screen-capture* constraints and have no
25	  bearing on a mic — don't reach for them here.)
26	- **Read the whole n-best list, not just alternative `[0]`.** Set
27	  `maxAlternatives` > 1 and iterate `result[0..length]` for `{ transcript,
28	  confidence }`; the ranked alternatives are exactly where homophone / near-miss
29	  recovery lives.
30	- **`onresult`, `onend`, and `onerror` all fire — settle the cycle exactly once.**
31	  Guard a `settled` flag: interim results arrive before the final one, a cycle can
32	  end with no result at all (treat `onend`-without-result as `no-speech`), and an
33	  error and an end can both arrive.
34	- **With `interimResults` off, engines omit `isFinal` — treat a result as final
35	  unless `isFinal === false`.** Don't test `if (result.isFinal)` (it's `undefined`
36	  on those engines and you'll drop every result); test `result.isFinal !== false`.
37	- **The classic recognizer streams audio to a cloud service (Google's) — plan for
38	  it.** A `network` error means "offline / service unreachable", and audio leaves
39	  the machine. On-device recognition is opt-in and capability-gated: probe
40	  `SpeechRecognition.available({ langs, processLocally: true }) === 'available'`
41	  once and cache it, set `recognizer.processLocally = true`, and **never trigger a
42	  language-pack download** (only `'available'` counts, not `'downloadable'`). When
43	  the local path is absent, fall back to ordinary cloud recognition unchanged.
44	- **Contextual biasing (`SpeechRecognitionPhrase` + `recognizer.phrases`) works
45	  only on the on-device path** — gate it behind that same availability probe and
46	  apply it best-effort (any failure falls back to un-biased recognition rather than
47	  breaking the listen cycle). Only bias **closed vocabularies you control**
48	  (a command lexicon, known labels, a spelling alphabet) with **modest** boosts:
49	  over-boosting makes the recognizer hear a biased phrase when the user actually
50	  said a same-sounding free-form utterance.
51	- **Map the raw Web Speech error names to a small taxonomy** — `not-allowed` /
52	  `service-not-allowed` → permission-denied, plus `no-speech`, `network`,
53	  `aborted`, `audio-capture`, else `other`. In particular `aborted` is the
54	  *self-inflicted* stop (you called `recognizer.abort()`), so the caller should
55	  ignore it rather than surface it as a failure.
56	- **A missed endpoint mid-utterance needs a pause watchdog, not just `onend`.**
57	  If interim hypotheses exist but no final arrives, the engine may have lost the
58	  endpoint; a timer that fires after a pause discards the half-heard input and
59	  reopens a fresh cycle (preventing "heart heart" doubles when the user repeats
60	  themselves). Set the threshold **well above a natural mid-command thinking
61	  pause** — a tight window (~1.2 s) cuts real commands; a wider one (~1.8 s) keeps
62	  only the genuine missed-endpoint case.
63	- **Mic permission is per-origin, and the grant belongs to whatever page the
64	  recognizer runs in.** In a content script the prompt reads as the *host site*
65	  asking and the grant persists for that origin. Surface it in a controlled moment:
66	  preflight `navigator.permissions.query({ name: 'microphone' })`, then a one-time
67	  `getUserMedia` to raise the prompt. **Retry the capture bare** (`{ audio: true }`)
68	  if the first constrained call is rejected — a browser balking at the constraint
69	  *shape* must not be misread as a permission denial; only a second failure is a
70	  real "denied".
71	
72	## Text-to-speech (`chrome.tts` / `speechSynthesis`)
73	
74	- **Prefer `chrome.tts` over `speechSynthesis` — it's immune to page
75	  autoplay / user-activation gating.** `speechSynthesis` invoked from a content
76	  script is subject to the host page's autoplay policy and can silently refuse to
77	  speak; `chrome.tts` (extension-only, needs the `"tts"` permission, usable from the
78	  service worker) is not. Make `chrome.tts` primary and `speechSynthesis` the
79	  fallback for non-extension document contexts.
80	- **`chrome.tts` doesn't exist in a content script — relay speak/cancel to the
81	  service worker over a port.** Keep the same `speak()`/`cancel()` contract on both
82	  sides; the in-page port sends `{ speak }` / `{ cancel }` messages and the worker
83	  drives `chrome.tts`. On port disconnect, resolve every pending `speak()` promise
84	  so a dead worker never leaves the caller awaiting an utterance that will never
85	  finish.
86	- **Voice lists load lazily — an empty `getVoices()` means "not ready yet", not
87	  "no voices".** Resolve the preferred voice on the *first* `speak()` and don't
88	  cache an empty result: fall back to the default that turn and try to resolve
89	  again next turn.
90	- **Don't trust the OS/browser default voice — it's often the most robotic one
91	  installed.** Keep an ordered list of preferred voice names, take the first one
92	  actually installed, and fall back to the default only when none match.
93	- **Resolve a `speak()` promise on *any* terminal event, and never reject.** For
94	  `chrome.tts` that's `end` / `interrupted` / `cancelled` / `error`; for
95	  `speechSynthesis` it's `onend` / `onerror`. Resolving (not rejecting) on error
96	  keeps a spoken-prompt sequence from deadlocking on one bad utterance. Use
97	  `enqueue: false` so a new line interrupts the current one for turn-taking rather
98	  than stacking up.
99	- **Neither engine reliably supports SSML — you can't force intonation.** If a
100	  punctuation cue matters (a question's rising tone), speak the cue in words
101	  ("question mark") rather than relying on prosody the engine may not apply.
102

1	# Chrome extensions
2	
3	Portable, project-agnostic practices for building Chrome (and Chromium) extensions — manifest
4	versions, background/service workers, content scripts, permissions, packaging and store review —
5	true for any extension read cold.
6	
7	> **Releasing, versioning, and Chrome Web Store publication are standardized** — before building
8	> or changing any release/publish machinery in an extension repo, read the
9	> [chrome-store-releases standard](skills/chrome-store-releases/SKILL.md) and copy its canonical
10	> workflows instead of re-deriving them.
11	
12	## Service worker
13	
14	- **Handing a path to a Chrome API or `fetch` from an MV3 service worker** (`importScripts`,
15	  `action.setIcon`) — make it extension-root absolute: a leading slash, or
16	  `chrome.runtime.getURL(...)`. A worker's relative paths resolve against the worker's **own** file
17	  location, not the extension root, and a bare relative path fails silently — it can abort the
18	  worker on import, or make an API call reject while the worker keeps running.
19	
20	- **Wanting `import`/`export` in extension code** — MV3 loads ES modules natively; don't add a
21	  bundler just to use them. Declare the service worker `"type": "module"` and load page/side-panel
22	  scripts with `<script type="module">`; relative imports resolve within the packaged extension.
23	  Content scripts are the exception — they are classic scripts, below.
24	
25	## Content scripts
26	
27	- **Assembling a shared global from several injected content-script files** — **augment** it,
28	  never replace it: merge onto it (e.g. `Object.assign`), not `globalThis.X = {...}`. The files are
29	  re-injected into the page on every activation (e.g. every popup open), so replacing makes each
30	  newly-injected file wipe what earlier files already attached.
31	
32	- **Accumulating state in a file that is re-injected** (e.g. a list a source pushes into) — reset
33	  it at load time.
34	
35	- **Loading ES module code into a content script** — register a tiny **classic loader** whose only
36	  statement is a *dynamic* `import(chrome.runtime.getURL('…'))`. A **registered or static content
37	  script runs as a *classic* script — it can't be an ES module**:
38	  `chrome.scripting.registerContentScripts` and static `content_scripts` inject their files as
39	  classic scripts (there is no `type: 'module'` mode, unlike a page's `<script type="module">` or
40	  the module service worker), so a top-level `import` in one throws
41	  `Uncaught SyntaxError: Cannot use import statement outside a module` — **in the host page's
42	  console, not the extension's**. Dynamic `import()` is legal in a classic script, and the module it
43	  pulls in runs in the same content-script isolated world with the content-script `chrome.*` surface
44	  intact.
45	
46	- **Adding an import to a content-script module** — list that module **and its whole transitive
47	  import graph** under `web_accessible_resources` (gated to the target origins), or the fetch is
48	  blocked.
49	
50	- **Keeping that `web_accessible_resources` list correct** — have a test walk the import graph
51	  from the entry module, so a newly-added import can't silently fall out of the list.
52	
53	## Permissions and host access
54	
55	- **Matching a host with `chrome.events.UrlFilter`** — its host operators are **raw string
56	  matches, not domain-boundary matches**: `hostSuffix: "example.com"` also matches
57	  `evilexample.com`, and `declarativeContent`'s `PageStateMatcher.pageUrl` gates an action icon or
58	  page condition on exactly these filters. To mean *apex-or-any-subdomain*, combine
59	  `hostEquals: "example.com"` with `hostSuffix: ".example.com"` (the leading dot forces a label
60	  boundary); never gate a security- or origin-sensitive behavior on a bare `hostSuffix`.
61	
62	- **Running a content script on arbitrary third-party pages without an install-time host warning**
63	  — request access at runtime: declare the origins under `optional_host_permissions` plus the
64	  (silent) `scripting` permission, call `chrome.permissions.request()` **synchronously inside a real
65	  foreground user gesture** (Chrome rejects the request from a service-worker message handler), then
66	  register the script dynamically with `chrome.scripting.registerContentScripts()` — never a
67	  static `content_scripts` entry.
68	
69	- **Starting the service worker when a runtime-granted permission is in play** — reconcile your
70	  stored enabled-flag against the permission actually granted and re-register (or clean up) to
71	  match, on every start. The grant can be revoked from `chrome://extensions` out from under you.
72	
73	- **A fetch to a host you listed failing in-browser** — `host_permissions` does not bypass CORS.
74	  Listing a host lets the extension's fetches *reach* it, but the server must still return CORS
75	  headers for the extension origin (`chrome-extension://<id>`) or the request fails.
76	
77	- **Reaching your *own* backend** — don't add a `host_permissions` entry merely for that: if it
78	  already returns permissive CORS the fetch succeeds without one, and the entry only adds a scary
79	  install-time host-access warning.
80	
81	## Sign-in and tokens
82	
83	- **Authenticating an extension to a JWT-validating backend** (an API Gateway JWT authorizer, any
84	  OIDC-validating server) — obtain a Google **ID token** with `chrome.identity.launchWebAuthFlow`
85	  (`response_type=id_token`) against a Google Cloud OAuth client of type **Web application**,
86	  redirect to `https://<extension-id>.chromiumapp.org/` (from `chrome.identity.getRedirectURL()`),
87	  scope `openid email profile`, and **verify the returned `nonce`**. Pin the extension id with a
88	  manifest `key` so the redirect URI stays fixed. Do **not** use `chrome.identity.getAuthToken` —
89	  it returns an opaque OAuth *access* token (no verifiable signature/`iss`/`aud`) that a JWT
90	  authorizer rejects.
91	
92	- **Refreshing a token silently** (`launchWebAuthFlow({interactive:false})`) — request
93	  `prompt=none`. `prompt=consent` always needs interaction and therefore always fails silently —
94	  reserve it (or omit `prompt`) for the interactive fallback.
95	
96	- **Refreshing silently with more than one account signed in** — pass the remembered account's
97	  email as `login_hint`; otherwise the provider can't tell which session to reuse and forces an
98	  interactive account-picker. Persist the non-secret email from the first successful sign-in.
99	
100	- **Storing a token** — extension storage is unencrypted, so treat tokens as secrets at rest: keep
101	  the bearer/ID token in in-memory `chrome.storage.session` (cleared on browser exit) and persist
102	  only non-secret identifiers (e.g. the account email) to `chrome.storage.local`.
103	
104	- **Wanting a token to survive a browser restart** — re-run the silent flow; don't switch to a
105	  refresh-token flow just for that, which puts a longer-lived credential on disk.
106	
107	## Extension UI surfaces
108	
109	- **Knowing whether your side panel is open** — have the panel open a `Port` on load and read its
110	  connect/disconnect as open/closed. MV3 gives the side panel no is-open/close API, and an action
111	  popup suppresses `action.onClicked`.
112	
113	- **Opening the side panel programmatically** — `chrome.sidePanel.open()` needs Chrome 116+, so
114	  raise `minimum_chrome_version` accordingly.
115	
116	- **Putting a menu on the toolbar icon itself** — create it with
117	  `chrome.contextMenus.create({ contexts: ['action'], … })`; the `contextMenus` permission carries
118	  **no** install-time warning (unlike a broad host permission).
119	
120	- **Recreating those menu items on install or startup** — call `contextMenus.removeAll()` first,
121	  so they self-heal instead of throwing on duplicate ids when the service worker re-runs its top
122	  level.
123	
124	## Introspecting a service worker over CDP
125	
126	- **Awaiting a `chrome.*` callback API inside `Runtime.evaluate`** — don't: they don't reliably
127	  settle when awaited with `awaitPromise: true` (a hang with no internal timeout). Build the awaited
128	  signal from plain promises (`fetch`/`OffscreenCanvas`) instead.
129	
130	- **Reading a worker value from an injected evaluate** — a bare top-level `function`/`const` isn't
131	  reachable from one, so expose what the probe reads as an explicit `globalThis.x = …`.
132	
133	- **Attaching to a dormant worker** — poll for the global rather than reading it once immediately
134	  after attaching. A dormant worker has no globals until it re-runs its top level, and attaching to
135	  it is what starts that.

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-branch-status: Assess one branch's landed status — merged, already-in-main, superseded, orphaned, or genuine unmerged work — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single branch is safe to delete, judging by content not the ref's name (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-branches task hands you branches to assess).
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
- writing-claudinite-skills: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus — SKILL.md conventions, where a skill's checks and tests live, catalog and pack wiring. Use when creating or editing a pack's skills/<name>/ in the canon; a consumer project's own agent docs are authoring-agent-docs' turf.
- writing-migration-plans: Where a plan and a design live, and how to order a plan's phases so nothing stalls mid-run — the plan is a tracking issue (never a plan document in the repo), the design doc carries only the end state with rationale and alternatives; front-load the out-of-band setup, write ALL the code including the cleanup and take one approval for the stack, then chain every execution step to the verification of the one before it as a queued continuation, and keep the tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan — including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file — and when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.mjs or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- canary-role: What ClaudiniteCanary is for and how to work in it — the live canary for Claudinite's consumer-safety gate. Use before changing anything in this repo, and when a canary rehearsal comes back red and you have to decide what the red means.
- git-github-advanced: Git/GitHub procedures beyond the baseline lifecycle. Use for commit layering, recovering a branch after a squash-merge, CI-trigger rules, GitHub Actions gotchas, or merge-relocation traps.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- merge-to-main: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
- site-visual-check: Screenshot and visually verify site/ (claudinite.com), desktop and mobile, and deliver the result to the owner. Use when changing site/ markup, CSS, or animations, or when checking responsive/mobile rendering.
- chrome-store-releases: The Chrome Web Store release standard every extension repo of ours ships — the vendored release workflows and composite actions, .github/release.config, versioning and the packaged artifact, the store secrets, the README install sections, and the manual Chrome Web Store steps. Use when setting up an extension repo to publish, changing or debugging its release pipeline, when asked to "bump version" on an extension repo, or when a cer/ check fires.
- bump-version: Raise the project's version — a minor bump by default. Use when the owner says "bump version".
- start-a-new-fringe-year: Set up and run the pipeline for a new Edinburgh Fringe year (a new years/<YYYY>/ folder). Use when asked to start, bootstrap, or plan a Fringe year the repo does not have data for yet — e.g. "set up 2027", "start next year".
- static-site-releases: The release standard every static-site repo of ours ships — the date-anchored version scheme, release-on-push, the explicit publish set, .github/site.config, the vendored workflows, the Pages deploy, and the setup a new site repo needs. Use when setting up a site repo, changing or debugging its release pipeline or site.config, when asked to "bump version" on a site repo, or when a static-website check fires.
- merge-and-ci: Drive this repo's PR-to-merged flow cheaply — when to open the PR, how to get CI green in a Claude web session, how to poll without wasting wall time or tokens, and when to arm auto-merge instead of waiting. Use whenever a session opens, watches, or lands a PR here — including one opened incidentally mid-task by an unattended or scheduled run, and any moment you ask "is CI green yet?" — not only for a deliberate merge or an e2e/heavy/UI change.
- snapshot-approval: Get owner approval for a moved UI-snapshot baseline. Use whenever a change to a dev/requirements case (its spec or its rendering) makes the snapshot tests fail — the pixels moved and the baseline wants to change.
- testing-guide: Map of this repo's test suites, the requirements model, and where each harness documents itself. Use before writing or changing tests here, adding a requirement case, or debugging a suite — the invariants live in the gcec pack's RULES.md; this is the deeper how-to.
- engineering-practices: General software-engineering practices — naming by scope, single-source-of-truth with drift guards, GENERATED-file discipline, earning each dependency, verifying real platform behavior. Use before writing or editing code.
- create-release-plan: The Firebase release standard — two separate dev/prod projects with the committed default pinned to dev, prod config injected only by the release pipeline, App Check attestation gating, and deliberate promotion. Use when planning a Firebase-backed app's first release, splitting a project into dev and prod, or wiring prod config and App Check into a release pipeline.
- paper-intake: Take a research paper PDF into references/ — folder, digest, extracted figures, cropped panels, calibration, synthesis. Use whenever a new article is added to this repo, or an existing one needs re-processing.
- vessel-overlay-review: Show a vessel-extraction result as an annotated overlay on the original panel and state explicit visual assertions about it. Use whenever proposing, revising, or reporting on the segmentation/measurement pipeline in this repo — before quoting any new numbers.
- map-a-data-source: Reconnaissance on a website you want data from but don't control — locate the real data surface (hydration blob, client API, or markup) and write the findings down before any parser exists. Use when adding a new source to a scraper, or when an existing source stops parsing and you suspect the site changed shape.
- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one — Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). 1	# browser-speech pack (local)
2	
3	A pack for the **browser speech surfaces**: `SpeechRecognition` / `webkitSpeechRecognition`,
4	`chrome.tts`, `speechSynthesis`, and the microphone capture behind them. Declared by hand as
5	`local/browser-speech` in `.claudinite-settings.json`.
6	
7	**Every rule judges a browser API contract, not a product decision.** Each one holds in any
8	voice-driven web app — nothing in a rule's logic, rationale, or fix text is specific to this
9	repo, and the scan is repo-shape agnostic (see below), so the pack cannot pass vacuously green
10	somewhere laid out differently. This repo is where the rules were *discovered* and is the corpus
11	they are verified against; it is not what they are about.
12	
13	**Why local, not a canon declaration:** the mounted canon shelf has no home for this facet. The
14	`chrome-extension` pack covers MV3 build/runtime gotchas and says nothing about speech;
15	`chrome-extension-release`, `node`, `github-actions`, `tidy-repo`, `spec-driven-product` and
16	`executable-requirements` are all orthogonal. Nothing here duplicates a canon rule.
17	
18	**Provenance:** distilled from this repo's real usage — `extension/src/speech/` (`stt-port.js`,
19	`tts-port.js`, `remote-tts-port.js`, `biasing.js`), the sequential action loop in
20	`extension/src/app/orchestrator.js`, decisions D2 and D11 in `dev/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`, the
21	`aec`/`od` diagnostics in `dev/docs/SESSION-LOG.md`, and the mic-teardown live check in issue
22	\#63. Nothing in it is invented.
23	
24	**Promotion note:** the checks are written to be lifted as-is — repo-shape agnostic scan, API
25	contracts only, no project identifiers in any rule's logic or messages — so the central promote
26	stage should be able to move them into a canon `browser-speech` (or `web-speech`) technology pack
27	with only the `doc:` paths rewritten. The `RULES.md` prose is the part still worth re-reading for
28	project coupling at promote time: some of it records tuning this product measured (the pause
29	window) rather than a fact of the API. Until then it lives here.
30	
31	## Checks
32	
33	| Check | Enforces (≤5 words) | Severity |
34	|---|---|---|
35	| `tts-speak-settles` | speak settles on every outcome | blocking |
36	| `stt-terminal-handlers` | recognizer wires onend and onerror | blocking |
37	| `mic-capture-released` | getUserMedia capture stops its tracks | blocking |
38	| `mic-constraints-not-screen-capture` | mic constraints exclude display-only ones | blocking |
39	| `stt-error-map-has-default` | error mapping has a catch-all | blocking |
40	| `stt-interim-results-gated` | interim results gated on isFinal | blocking |
41	
42	**Scope.** All six scan any browser source file (`.js/.mjs/.cjs/.ts/.tsx/.jsx`) except test and
43	vendor paths — never a hard-coded project root. Each rule is already gated on the speech API it
44	judges actually appearing in the file, so the API usage *is* the trigger and the scan can be
45	repo-shaped; a path scope wired to one layout would make every rule match zero files and pass
46	vacuously green elsewhere, which is the worst failure mode a check has. The exclusion that
47	matters — test scaffolding, whose hand-rolled speech fakes implement only the halves of a
48	contract a given case needs — is stated directly, by test/vendor path and test filename.
49	
50	**Parsed, not grepped, where the name alone doesn't decide it.**
51	`mic-constraints-not-screen-capture` judges `suppressLocalAudioPlayback` / `restrictOwnAudio` only
52	where they *reach* a microphone capture — the balanced argument list of a `getUserMedia(` call,
53	plus one hop into a same-file constant that list names (hoisting constraints into a frozen
54	constant is how real code writes them). Every other use of those names is legitimate: a real
55	`getDisplayMedia` call, a `getSupportedConstraints()` probe, a comment explaining the trap — all
56	of which a file-wide grep would false-alarm on, this repo's own `stt-port.js` included.
57	
58	`stt-error-map-has-default` reads a switch's arms at the switch body's *own* brace depth, so a
59	nested switch's `default:` is not mistaken for the outer mapping's catch-all — and it treats a
60	`return`/`throw` immediately after the switch as the catch-all it is, since that is the other
61	idiomatic way to write a total mapping. It judges only switches whose arms `return` a kind: a
62	switch dispatching side effects over error names is a different shape, and the rule has no
63	honest opinion about its missing arm.
64	
65	`stt-interim-results-gated` reads the *value* assigned to `interimResults` rather than the name:
66	an explicit `= false` turns the flag off, every result is then final, and there is nothing to
67	gate — while a computed flag (`rec.interimResults = pauseResetMs > 0`, the shape real code takes)
68	counts as on, since a check cannot show it is off and the handler has to survive it being true.
69	It also judges only a file that spells its result handler out: a config module that sets the flag
70	and hands the recognizer on, and `rec.onresult = this.handleResult`, both keep their gate in a
71	file this check is not looking at, so delegation is answered with silence rather than a guess.
72	
73	**Both DOM wiring forms count.** `el.onend = …` and `el.addEventListener('end', …)` are equally
74	correct, so every handler rule accepts either (`lib.mjs` `wires`). A rule that knew only the
75	property form would silently pass half the world's code and false-alarm on any file mixing the
76	two.
77	
78	Red-first fixtures live in `pack.test.mjs`: each rule is run against a violating source and a
79	clean one — in both wiring forms, and in TypeScript under a plain `src/` as well as JavaScript —
80	and then against this repo's real `extension/src/` tree, which must stay quiet. The project's
81	vitest run picks the file up via the `.claudinite/local/packs/**/*.test.mjs` include in
82	`vitest.config.js`, so the checks ship green in CI.
83	
84	**When a check's whole point is precision, red-first has to prove it in two directions.** A
85	violating fixture failing and a clean one passing only proves the shipped check is correct — it
86	says nothing about whether the parsing it does was *necessary*. Also run the quiet fixtures
87	against the naive alternative the parsing exists to avoid (here: a file-wide grep in place of the
88	`getUserMedia(` scoping) and confirm they'd wrongly fire — that's what earns the parsing its
89	complexity. `mic-constraints-not-screen-capture`'s fixtures do both: the three firing fixtures
90	fail with the rule neutered, and the three quiet fixtures — plus this repo's own `stt-port.js` —
91	fail against a naive whole-file grep. `stt-error-map-has-default`'s do the same: its three firing
92	fixtures fail with the rule neutered, and against a naive "≥2 error names and no `default:`
93	anywhere in the file" grep the trailing-`return`, side-effect-dispatch and comment-only fixtures
94	all wrongly fire while the nested-switch violation goes undetected.
95	`stt-interim-results-gated`'s do the same: with its `isFinal` gate neutered both the clean fixture
96	*and this repo's own `stt-port.js`* fire — which is what proves the rule reaches the real file
97	rather than passing over it — and against a naive "mentions `interimResults`, never `isFinal`"
98	grep the flag-off, config-module, delegated-handler and comment-only fixtures all wrongly fire.
99	
100	## Prose (`RULES.md`)
101	
102	| Rule (≤5 words) | How enforced |
103	|---|---|
104	| chrome.tts unavailable to content scripts | prose |
105	| recognizer takes no audio constraints | prose (its display-only-constraint trap is checked) |
106	| preflight the mic deliberately | prose |
107	| endpointing fails; monitor mid-utterance pauses | prose (that interim results aren't delivered is checked) |
108	| biasing is on-device only | prose |
109	| voices load lazily; default is worst | prose |
110	| map speech errors to a taxonomy | prose (that the mapping is total is checked) |

1	# Browser speech — the judgment core
2	
3	Driving the browser's speech surfaces (`SpeechRecognition` / `webkitSpeechRecognition`,
4	`chrome.tts`, `speechSynthesis`, the mic capture behind them). The mechanical rules — completion
5	handlers, mic release, which constraints a mic capture may even ask for, whether an error mapping
6	is total, and whether interim hypotheses are gated before delivery — are this pack's six checks;
7	what follows is only what no check can decide for you.
8	
9	Each rule below is a judgment about the API, and holds for any voice-driven app. Where one cites
10	this repo — a file, a decision record, a measured number — that is the **evidence** it was drawn
11	from, not the scope it applies to; a rule grounded in a real instance beats one asserted in the
12	abstract. The measured values (the pause window especially) are this product's and should be
13	re-measured elsewhere, not copied.
14	
15	The one thing to keep in mind everywhere below: **speech failures are silent**. Nothing throws,
16	nothing logs, the UI keeps showing a live session — the user just hears nothing, or is heard by
17	nobody. Design each of these surfaces so every path produces exactly one observable outcome.
18	
19	## Where each API can run
20	
21	- `chrome.tts` is **not exposed to content scripts**. The session lives in the page (speech
22	  recognition needs a document, and the mic grant belongs to nytimes.com), so speaking is a
23	  relay: the content script sends `cc:speak` over the long-lived `cc-session` port and the
24	  service worker calls `chrome.tts` — `speech/remote-tts-port.js` presents the same contract as
25	  `speech/tts-port.js` so the orchestrator can't tell the difference. Prefer `chrome.tts` over
26	  `speechSynthesis` because it is immune to the page's autoplay rules (decision D2).
27	
28	## Self-echo is an application problem, not a constraints problem
29	
30	`webkitSpeechRecognition` **owns its own capture and exposes no hook for
31	`MediaTrackConstraints`** — you cannot ask the recognizer for echo cancellation. Chrome applies
32	its default AEC (a loopback of playout audio) to that capture, which already attenuates
33	`speechSynthesis`, but it misses `chrome.tts`'s OS-rendered output. So the residual echo is
34	handled at the app level by a string-match echo guard (REQ-SPCH-005), and that is the design,
35	not a stopgap (decision D11).
36	
37	Two traps around this:
38	
39	- `suppressLocalAudioPlayback` and `restrictOwnAudio` read like the fix for this and are not:
40	  they are **`getDisplayMedia` screen-capture** constraints, filtering a captured tab's own
41	  playout out of that tab's track, and `getUserMedia` ignores them without a word. The cost of
42	  reaching for one is not the dead property — it is that the echo guard that would have worked
43	  never gets written. (Enforced by the `mic-constraints-not-screen-capture` check.)
44	- The constraints you *can* set (`echoCancellation`, `noiseSuppression`, `autoGainControl`)
45	  apply only to the one capture you own — the permission preflight.
46	
47	## Ask for the microphone in a moment you chose
48	
49	Surface the permission prompt deliberately, with a short warm-up `getUserMedia` — not as a side
50	effect of the first listen cycle. Two rules for that preflight:
51	
52	- **Run it even when permission is already granted.** Otherwise the device is only warmed, and
53	  AEC engagement only known, on the very first grant.
54	- **Retry once bare when the constrained call rejects.** A rejection is either a real denial or
55	  a browser balking at the constraint shape; only a second failure is a genuine denial. Reading
56	  a constraint quirk as "mic denied" ends the session for no reason.
57	
58	(The capture must then be released on every path — that is the `mic-capture-released` check.)
59	
60	## Endpointing is unreliable — plan for the miss
61	
62	Chrome decides on its own when an utterance ended, and it does get it wrong: interim hypotheses
63	keep arriving and no final result ever lands. Left alone the user repeats themselves and you get
64	`"heart heart"`. The fix is a pause monitor that discards the half-heard input and reopens a
65	fresh cycle — with interim results used **only** as the "still speaking" signal, never delivered
66	to the caller. (That last half is the `stt-interim-results-gated` check; the monitor itself, and
67	the window below, are yours.)
68	
69	Tune the window from real sessions, not from taste: 1.2 s cut real commands off solvers who
70	paused to think mid-instruction; 1.8 s keeps only the genuine missed-endpoint case. Anything
71	that ships an audible cue for the reset needs the same care — it fires often.
72	
73	## Contextual biasing exists only on the on-device path
74	
75	`SpeechRecognitionPhrase` / `processLocally` work only where Chrome has an on-device model.
76	Treat biasing as strictly best-effort:
77	
78	- probe availability **once** and memoize the promise;
79	- accept only the literal `'available'` — never trigger a language-pack download;
80	- apply phrases inside a `try` and fall through to un-biased recognition on any failure;
81	- keep the un-biased path byte-for-byte unchanged (don't make every caller await a probe it
82	  doesn't need).
83	
84	## Voices load lazily, and the default one is usually the worst
85	
86	`getVoices()` returning an empty list means *"not ready yet"*, not *"no voices"* — resolve the
87	voice on first speak and, on an empty list, use the default and try again next time rather than
88	caching the empty answer. The OS default is often the most robotic voice installed, so carry an
89	ordered preference list and take the first installed match. That list is **taste, and taste has
90	been wrong here before** (`Google US English` led it, sounded bad, and was demoted): treat both
91	the voice order and the speaking rate as user-facing settings with a modest default, not as
92	constants to tune once.
93	
94	## Give recognition errors a taxonomy
95	
96	Map the raw Web Speech error names onto a small named set the dialog policy can reason about,
97	and keep the mapping in one place. The policy cares about *kinds* — nothing heard, the mic was
98	refused, we aborted on purpose, the network went — not about spellings, and a `default → other`
99	arm means a browser inventing a new name degrades instead of crashing. (That the mapping is
100	total is the `stt-error-map-has-default` check; choosing the kinds, and keeping them in one
101	place, is not.) Log the codes short (`en`/`ed`/`ea`…) so a whole session fits in a diagnostics
102	dump.
103

1	# host-page-adaptation pack (local)
2	
3	A pack for **being a guest in a web app you do not own**: reading its DOM, driving it with
4	synthetic input, watching it change, injecting your own UI into its chrome, and surviving the
5	day it is redesigned. Declared by hand as `local/host-page-adaptation` in
6	`.claudinite-settings.json`.
7	
8	**Every rule judges a DOM/API contract, not a product decision.** Each one holds for any code
9	driving a third-party page — a userscript, a browser-automation layer, an extension's content
10	script — and nothing in a rule's logic, rationale or fix text is specific to this repo. The scan
11	is repo-shape agnostic (see below), so the pack cannot pass vacuously green somewhere laid out
12	differently. This repo is where the rules were *discovered* and is the corpus they are verified
13	against; it is not what they are about.
14	
15	**Why local, not a canon declaration:** the mounted canon shelf has no home for this facet. The
16	`chrome-extension` pack covers MV3 *mechanics* — manifest, permissions, how a content script is
17	registered and why it can't be an ES module — i.e. how your code reaches the page; it says
18	nothing about what to do once it is there. `chrome-extension-release`, `node`,
19	`github-actions`, `tidy-repo`, `spec-driven-product`, `executable-requirements` and `barriers`
20	are orthogonal, and the sibling local pack `browser-speech` owns the speech surfaces, not the
21	page. Nothing here duplicates a canon rule.
22	
23	**Provenance:** distilled from this repo's real usage — the whole of
24	`extension/src/page-adapter/` (`selectors.js`, `reader.js`, `writer.js`, `watcher.js`,
25	`probe.js`, `splash.js`, `session-button.js`), the REQ-PAGE and REQ-LIFE requirement families
26	in `dev/docs/REQUIREMENTS.md`, the quarantine rule REQ-PAGE-011 and its arch test
27	(`extension-test/unit/arch.test.js`), the live-page findings recorded in `writer.js` (MT-02) and
28	in `selectors.js`'s dated verification notes, and the fake-host fixture
29	(`extension-test/fixtures/fake-nyt/`). Nothing in it is invented.
30	
31	**Promotion note:** the checks are written to be lifted as-is — repo-shape agnostic scan, DOM
32	contracts only, no project identifiers in any rule's logic or messages — so the central promote
33	stage should be able to move them into a canon pack for this facet (`host-page-adaptation`, or
34	whatever a canon `html`/DOM pack calls it) with only the `doc:` paths rewritten. The `RULES.md`
35	prose is the part still worth re-reading for project coupling at promote time: several rules
36	cite this host's specific behaviours (the ~30 s idle auto-pause, the pencil button with no
37	readable state) as evidence, and those are examples of a category, not constants.
38	
39	## Checks
40	
41	| Check | Enforces (≤5 words) | Severity |
42	|---|---|---|
43	| `page-observers-disconnected` | started DOM observers get disconnected | blocking |
44	| `synthetic-input-events-bubble` | dispatched input events set bubbles | blocking |
45	
46	**Scope.** Both scan any browser source file (`.js/.mjs/.cjs/.ts/.tsx/.jsx`) except test
47	and vendor paths — never a hard-coded project root. Each rule is gated on the DOM API it judges
48	actually appearing in the file, so the API usage *is* the trigger and the scan can be
49	repo-shaped; a path scope wired to one layout would make every rule match zero files and pass
50	vacuously green elsewhere, which is the worst failure mode a check has. The exclusion that
51	matters is test scaffolding: a test dispatching a bare event at its own jsdom node, or spinning
52	an observer it lets the runner collect, is doing something purpose-built and is not adapting to
53	a host page.
54	
55	**Parsed, not grepped, where the name alone doesn't decide it.**
56	
57	`synthetic-input-events-bubble` judges only events that are actually **dispatched** (a probe
58	event constructed to feature-detect is not input), only the interfaces that model **real user
59	input** (a `CustomEvent` is your own signal to your own listener and is legitimately
60	non-bubbling), and it resolves each side of the dispatch through **one hop**: the constructor
61	through an alias (`const Ctor = isKey ? view.KeyboardEvent : view.MouseEvent` is how a generic
62	`fire()` helper is written, and this repo's single dispatch site is exactly that shape), and
63	the dispatched value through a local (`const ev = new MouseEvent('click');
64	el.dispatchEvent(ev)` is the other shape real dispatch code takes). An init that spreads
65	(`{ ...init }`) without an explicit `bubbles:` is beyond what the rule can see, so it stays
66	silent there: the caller may well set the field, and a check that guessed would false-alarm on
67	precisely the well-factored helper that centralises this.
68	
69	**A third check was cut at review.** `synthetic-key-events-legacy-fields` (a synthetic
70	`KeyboardEvent` init must carry `keyCode`/`which`) enforced a real live-page lesson (MT-02) —
71	but this repo's only key-event construction builds its init in a helper and spreads it at the
72	one dispatch site, exactly the shape a spread-silent check can never read. A check that is
73	structurally blind to the house pattern can only ever fire on code that bypasses the `fire()`
74	helper, and the mistake in that code is the bypass, not the field it then forgot. The lesson
75	lands as prose instead (`RULES.md`, "A synthetic keystroke must carry the fields a real one
76	would").
77	
78	`page-observers-disconnected` is deliberately **file-scoped, not flow-scoped**: proving a
79	particular observer is disconnected on every path needs real data-flow analysis, and a check
80	that guesses is worse than one that asks a simple, honest question — "this file starts an
81	observer on the page; does it anywhere disconnect one?". An observer constructed but never
82	`.observe(`d has started nothing and is not asked.
83	
84	Red-first fixtures live in `pack.test.mjs`: each rule is run against violating sources and
85	clean ones — in both the direct and the aliased-constructor form, in TypeScript under a plain
86	`src/` as well as JavaScript — and then against this repo's real `extension/src/` tree, which
87	must stay quiet. The project's vitest run picks the file up via the
88	`.claudinite/local/packs/**/*.test.mjs` include in `vitest.config.js`, so the checks ship green
89	in CI.
90	
91	**When a check's whole point is precision, red-first has to prove it in two directions.** A
92	violating fixture failing and a clean one passing only proves the shipped check is correct — it
93	says nothing about whether the parsing it does was *necessary*. So the quiet fixtures are also
94	run against the naive alternative each piece of parsing exists to avoid, and confirmed to fire
95	there: a whole-file `new …Event(` grep wrongly flags the `CustomEvent`, never-dispatched and
96	already-bubbling cases.
97	
98	## Prose (`RULES.md`)
99	
100	| Rule (≤5 words) | How enforced |
101	|---|---|
102	| quarantine host DOM in one module | prose |
103	| identify host UI by nets | prose |
104	| date what selectors were verified against | prose |
105	| probe reports, never throws | prose |
106	| mirror the host in a fixture | prose |
107	| never trust a write; re-read | prose |
108	| synthetic keystrokes carry real-event fields | prose (its bubbles half is checked) |
109	| restore borrowed host state; degrade | prose |
110	| host lifecycle states aren't user actions | prose |
111	| be inert when off | prose (its observer teardown is checked) |
