1	# Adapting to a host page — the judgment core
2	
3	Working inside a web app you do not own: reading its DOM, driving it with synthetic input,
4	watching it change, and putting your own UI into its chrome. The mechanical rules — that a
5	page observer is disconnected, that a synthetic input event bubbles — are this pack's two
6	checks; what follows is only what no check can decide for you.
7	
8	Each rule below is a judgment about being a guest in someone else's page, and holds for any
9	code that does it — a userscript, an automation layer, an extension's content script. Where
10	one cites this repo — a file, a requirement id, a date — that is the **evidence** it was drawn
11	from, not the scope it applies to.
12	
13	The premise underneath all of it: **the host will change its markup without telling you, and
14	your code will not throw when it does.** A selector that matches nothing returns null; a click
15	on a renamed button never happens. Every rule here is about making that failure loud, local,
16	and cheap to fix.
17	
18	## Quarantine the host's DOM knowledge in one module
19	
20	All of it, behind an interface expressed in your own vocabulary — here `page-adapter/` returns
21	a `Snapshot` and takes `enterAnswer`, and the crossword model, the dialog policy and the
22	matcher never learn that the page exists (REQ-PAGE-011, `dev/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` §2). Two
23	things follow, and both are worth the discipline:
24	
25	- A redesign is a **one-directory** change, and the blast radius is knowable before you start.
26	- The rest of the codebase becomes testable without a browser at all — the pure layers here
27	  (`puzzle-model/`, `matching/`, `conversation/`) are pure *because* the quarantine holds.
28	
29	Inside that module, put **every selector and class string in one file**, and change values only
30	there (`page-adapter/selectors.js`). A selector inlined at its use site is the one that gets
31	missed when the host renames a class.
32	
33	Enforce the quarantine mechanically, by token: the repo's arch test fails if the host's class
34	prefix (`xwd__`) appears in code outside `page-adapter/`.
35	
36	## Identify host UI by a net, not by a selector
37	
38	A single selector is a bet that one class name survives. Cast a net instead, and make the last
39	strand semantic:
40	
41	- class nets that accept a family (`[class*="xwd__toolbar"]`), not one exact name;
42	- attribute and role hooks the host is less likely to churn (`role="cell"`, `data-testid`,
43	  `aria-label`);
44	- and a **text/shape fallback** underneath: the splash is found by class net *or* by "a visible
45	  container whose text says 'Ready to start solving' with a Play-ish button in it, whatever its
46	  classes are called" (`page-adapter/splash.js`); the pause veil is found by its copy plus
47	  visibility (`reader.js isPaused`).
48	
49	Visibility is part of identity. Hosts keep dismissed modals in the DOM, so a match that ignores
50	`display`/`visibility`/zero-size will keep reporting a splash you already cleared.
51	
52	## Write down what you verified the selectors against, and when
53	
54	The selectors file is the only place in the codebase whose truth lives on someone else's
55	server, so it carries its own provenance: the date and page it was last verified against, the
56	captured markup it was read from, and — most valuable — the **negative** findings.
57	`selectors.js` records that the state classes sit on the `<rect>` and not the `<g>`, that the
58	pencil button exposes no `aria-pressed` and no class change, that the letter/number `<text>`
59	nodes carry no distinguishing classes and the class-based selectors match nothing live. Each of
60	those is an hour of somebody's life, and none of it is recoverable from the code.
61	
62	## Ship a probe, and make a broken page a finding rather than an exception
63	
64	One entry point that reports the health of every selector against the live page —
65	`page-adapter/probe.js`, REQ-PAGE-009, run from the in-page menu (MT-01). It is the first thing
66	to run when a user says "it stopped working", and it turns "the extension is broken" into "the
67	clue-list wrapper selector matches 0, want 2".
68	
69	It must **never throw**: a probe that dies on the first missing element reports one fault and
70	hides the other nine. Collect a row per selector and return them all — and have it capture
71	forensics for the things you could *not* read (the probe here dumps the pencil button's
72	attributes precisely because its ON state has never been readable), so the next report arrives
73	with the evidence already in it.
74	
75	## Mirror the host in a fixture, and let the fixture define the expected shape
76	
77	A saved, simplified copy of the host page (`extension-test/fixtures/fake-nyt/`, served by
78	`npm run fixture`) mirrors the selectors exactly, and the integration tests drive that. It buys
79	two things a live page cannot: the read/write/watch cycle is testable in CI at all, and the
80	whole voice loop is rehearsable locally without a subscription (`npm run build:dev` widens the
81	matches to `localhost:8787`, MT-23).
82	
83	Its limit is the same as its virtue — **the fixture only ever shows you the markup you already
84	knew about**, so a passing suite is never evidence about the live page. Keep a manual-test
85	document for what only the real host can answer (`dev/docs/MANUAL-TESTS.md`), and treat every
86	live finding as a fixture update.
87	
88	## Never trust a write — verify by re-reading
89	
90	Address the target by position rather than relying on the host's own cursor conventions (click
91	each cell, then type one letter — immune to the host's advance-on-type and skip-filled
92	settings), then **read the DOM back and confirm what you meant is there** (REQ-PAGE-007). The
93	host may ignore untrusted events, may auto-advance differently than you assumed, may reject the
94	input silently; the re-read is the only thing that distinguishes those from success.
95	
96	Poll the re-read, don't do it synchronously after the last dispatch: the host renders
97	asynchronously (React here), so the DOM immediately after your event is the DOM *before* the
98	app processed it. And aim your events at a node **inside the app's own subtree** — the selected
99	element if it has focus, otherwise a known app node. A modern app delegates key handling near
100	its root, which is a descendant of `<body>`, so an event dispatched at `document` or `body`
101	bubbles *past* it and is never seen (`page-adapter/writer.js`).
102	
103	## A synthetic keystroke must carry the fields a real one would
104	
105	The browser fills in the deprecated `keyCode`/`which`/`charCode` on every real keystroke; on
106	a synthetic one they are plain init fields that default to 0, so
107	`new KeyboardEvent('keydown', { key: 'A' })` reaches the page as a keystroke whose keyCode is
108	0. Deprecated is not the same as unread: hosts with a long-lived key-handling layer still
109	branch on the legacy fields — this one does (verified live, MT-02) — and a 0 matches nothing,
110	so the handler runs and nothing happens, indistinguishable from "the app ignores untrusted
111	events". Mirror the real event instead: `keyCode` and `which` alongside `key`/`code`,
112	`charCode` on `keypress`, and the full keydown → keypress → keyup sequence a real keystroke
113	produces (`page-adapter/writer.js` `keyEventInit`/`typeKey`).
114	
115	Build the init in **one helper** and spread it at the single dispatch site, so fidelity is one
116	function's job. That factoring is also why this rule is prose rather than a check: the init a
117	well-factored adapter dispatches is opaque to a static scan (`{ ...init }` could carry
118	anything), so a check here could only ever police code that bypasses the helper — and the
119	mistake in that code is bypassing the helper, not the field it then forgot.
120	
121	## Put back any host state you borrowed, and degrade when you cannot read it
122	
123	Driving a host toggle means driving it back: pencil mode is set to match the write and restored
124	afterwards, so the user's own typing mode is never stolen (REQ-PAGE-012).
125	
126	You will often be unable to read the state you are toggling — the live pencil button has no
127	`aria-pressed` and no class change, so "on or off?" is genuinely unanswerable. Design for the
128	unreadable case as the **normal** one, not the error case: fall back to click parity, and let
129	the feature that depends on it degrade (the letters still land; only the pencil softening is
130	lost, REQ-ANS-019) rather than failing the operation.
131	
132	## The host has a lifecycle of its own, and its blank states are not your user's doing
133	
134	You are sharing the page with an app that has its own timers, veils and modals, and each one
135	looks like something else from inside your adapter:
136	
137	- **Idle timers.** This host auto-pauses a quiet puzzle after ~30 s of no keyboard input. A
138	  voice solver touches no keyboard, so the adapter sends a bare `Shift` keydown/keyup on every
139	  heard command — a real key event that types nothing and moves nothing (REQ-LIFE-017). Choose
140	  the nudge so it cannot mutate state, and drive it from real user activity, never from a timer
141	  of your own: when the user really has gone quiet, the host *should* pause and your session
142	  should end with it.
143	- **Veils that blank the content.** The pause veil empties the visible entries. A change watcher
144	  that diffs first and checks for the veil second will read that as the user clearing the whole
145	  grid. Check for the host's own overlay states **before** diffing, report the state once, and
146	  return (`page-adapter/watcher.js`).
147	- **Pre-content splashes.** The board may not exist for minutes while a "Ready to start
148	  solving?" modal is up. Absence of the content is not absence of the app.
149	
150	## Be inert when you are off
151	
152	Your code loads on the host's page whether or not the user is using you, so **doing nothing is
153	the resting state** (REQ-NFR-004). Watchers are created on demand and stopped with the session;
154	nothing polls; nothing observes between sessions.
155	
156	Keep load-time page changes to an explicit, minimal carve-out — here exactly one: mounting the
157	toolbar button (REQ-LIFE-012). Mount it by waiting with a `MutationObserver` that **disconnects
158	the moment the element lands** (the `page-observers-disconnected` check), and give up only when
159	the host shows no app markup at all — a slow render or a splash must not cost you the button,
160	but an archive page must not leave you waiting forever.
161

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-branch-status: Assess one branch's landed status — merged, already-in-main, superseded, orphaned, or genuine unmerged work — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single branch is safe to delete, judging by content not the ref's name (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-branches task hands you branches to assess).
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
- writing-claudinite-skills: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus — SKILL.md conventions, where a skill's checks and tests live, catalog and pack wiring. Use when creating or editing a pack's skills/<name>/ in the canon; a consumer project's own agent docs are authoring-agent-docs' turf.
- writing-migration-plans: Where a plan and a design live, and how to order a plan's phases so nothing stalls mid-run — the plan is a tracking issue (never a plan document in the repo), the design doc carries only the end state with rationale and alternatives; front-load the out-of-band setup, write ALL the code including the cleanup and take one approval for the stack, then chain every execution step to the verification of the one before it as a queued continuation, and keep the tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan — including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file — and when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.mjs or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- canary-role: What ClaudiniteCanary is for and how to work in it — the live canary for Claudinite's consumer-safety gate. Use before changing anything in this repo, and when a canary rehearsal comes back red and you have to decide what the red means.
- git-github-advanced: Git/GitHub procedures beyond the baseline lifecycle. Use for commit layering, recovering a branch after a squash-merge, CI-trigger rules, GitHub Actions gotchas, or merge-relocation traps.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- merge-to-main: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
- site-visual-check: Screenshot and visually verify site/ (claudinite.com), desktop and mobile, and deliver the result to the owner. Use when changing site/ markup, CSS, or animations, or when checking responsive/mobile rendering.
- chrome-store-releases: The Chrome Web Store release standard every extension repo of ours ships — the vendored release workflows and composite actions, .github/release.config, versioning and the packaged artifact, the store secrets, the README install sections, and the manual Chrome Web Store steps. Use when setting up an extension repo to publish, changing or debugging its release pipeline, when asked to "bump version" on an extension repo, or when a cer/ check fires.
- bump-version: Raise the project's version — a minor bump by default. Use when the owner says "bump version".
- start-a-new-fringe-year: Set up and run the pipeline for a new Edinburgh Fringe year (a new years/<YYYY>/ folder). Use when asked to start, bootstrap, or plan a Fringe year the repo does not have data for yet — e.g. "set up 2027", "start next year".
- static-site-releases: The release standard every static-site repo of ours ships — the date-anchored version scheme, release-on-push, the explicit publish set, .github/site.config, the vendored workflows, the Pages deploy, and the setup a new site repo needs. 1	import { finding } from '../../../shared/engine/checks/helpers/findings.mjs';
2	import { classificationLine, classesIn } from '../../../shared/engine/checks/helpers/session-transcript.mjs';
3	
4	// The testable half of RULES.md's "Put the `Comment class:` line on its own
5	// line": the classifier reads the WHOLE classification line and adds EVERY class
6	// token it finds (`classesIn()` matches globally), so the natural-sounding
7	//     Comment class: other — not a correction, feature request, or process-change
8	// declares all four classes, not `other`. The stray `feature` then arms
9	// `feature-requirements-first` BLOCKING against whatever commits the branch
10	// carries, even when the session never touched a product feature.
11	//
12	// This asserts the MANDATED FORM, not the author's intent. The prose tells the
13	// agent to write the class alone and put any explanation on the next line, so
14	// the line either is that or it is not — a question every character of it
15	// answers. An earlier draft chased intent instead, firing only on a class token
16	// that followed a negation word from a hand-picked list ("not", "never",
17	// "besides", …). That is unbounded in the wrong direction: the harm comes from a
18	// class token being PRESENT, and prose smuggles them in without negating
19	// anything. Probed against the real helper, that draft stayed silent on
20	//     Comment class: other — unrelated to any feature request      (declares feature)
21	//     Comment class: other, setting the feature question aside     (declares feature)
22	//     Comment class: correction | feature | process-change | other (declares all four)
23	// — the last a verbatim paste of the menu out of the classifier's own prompt,
24	// i.e. the likeliest way this bug is reproduced, missed by the check named for
25	// it. Checking the form catches all three and needs no word list, because a
26	// conforming line has nowhere to hide a token.
27	//
28	// A genuinely mixed comment stays legal and stays silent: it names each part it
29	// really is, positively, on that one line (`Comment class: correction,
30	// process-change`). Whether four comma-separated classes are "honest" is exactly
31	// the intent judgment this rule refuses to make — the form is respected, so the
32	// classifier does what the line asked.
33	//
34	// ADVISORY, deliberately, where the underlying defect is blocking-grade: the
35	// transcript is append-only, so by the time this is observable the declaration
36	// cannot be retracted. A blocking finding could never converge — it would spend
37	// the session's Stop cycles on something no edit can fix, which is precisely the
38	// waste the lesson records. Its job is to name the cause the moment it appears
39	// so the session doesn't re-derive it from an unexplained
40	// `feature-requirements-first` failure.
41	
42	// One class token, spelled as the classifier's own alternation spells it, so
43	// this check models what `classesIn()` sees rather than a second opinion of it.
44	const CLASS = String.raw`(?:correction|feature|process[\s-]change|other)`;
45	// The mandated form: class tokens joined by a declaration separator, nothing
46	// else. `|` is deliberately NOT a separator — it is how the prompt renders the
47	// menu, so pasting the menu verbatim fails this pattern rather than reading as
48	// a four-class declaration.
49	const CONFORMING_RE = new RegExp(String.raw`^\s*${CLASS}(?:\s*(?:,|&|\+|and)\s*${CLASS})*\s*\.?\s*$`, 'i');
50	
51	const rule = {
52	  id: 'tldr/comment-class-menu',
53	  severity: 'advisory',
54	  description: 'The `Comment class:` line must carry the class alone — every class token on it is declared, however the line phrases them',
55	  doc: '.claudinite/local/packs/tldr/RULES.md',
56	  scope: 'work',
57	  why: 'the classifier adds every class token on the classification line, so any explanation sharing that line declares the classes it mentions — a stray `feature` arms feature-requirements-first BLOCKING against the branch even when no product feature was touched',
58	
59	  run(work) {
60	    // Only the latest owner turn is judged, for the same reason
61	    // comment-classification judges only that one: the transcript is
62	    // append-only, so an earlier turn's line was already reported at its own
63	    // Stop and can never converge.
64	    const turn = work.conversation().ownerTurns().last();
65	    if (!turn.exists) return [];
66	    const line = classificationLine(turn.reply());
67	    // No classification line at all is comment-classification's finding, not this one.
68	    if (!line) return [];
69	
70	    // Everything after the `Comment class:` colon — the prefix cannot contain
71	    // one (the helper's pattern forbids it), so the first colon is the split.
72	    const declaration = line.slice(line.indexOf(':') + 1);
73	    if (CONFORMING_RE.test(declaration)) return [];
74	
75	    const declared = [...classesIn(declaration)].sort();
76	    // A line naming no class at all is unclassified — comment-classification's
77	    // finding, not this one.
78	    if (!declared.length) return [];
79	
80	    const arms = declared.includes('feature')
81	      ? ', including `feature`, which arms `feature-requirements-first` BLOCKING against this branch'
82	      : '';
83	
84	    return [finding(rule, {
85	      file: '(conversation)',
86	      what: `the \`Comment class:\` line carries more than the class it means, so the classifier reads it as declaring ${declared.map((c) => `\`${c}\``).join(', ')}${arms}`,
87	      fix: 'write the class alone on its own line — `Comment class: other` — and put any explanation on the NEXT line; a genuinely mixed comment names each part it really is, comma-separated, on that one line. The transcript is append-only, so re-declaring cleanly on a later line does not override this one — do not retry, and expect the declared classes\' rules to fire on this branch',
88	    })];
89	  },
90	};
91	
92	export default rule;
93

3	// A VENDORED workflow under `.github/workflows/` carries this repo's one
4	// deliberate delta over its canon stub: a step that aligns the repo-root
5	// package.json to a version the pipeline just bumped. It is load-bearing — the
6	// release config only bumps `manifest_path` and `package_json_path`, so without
7	// it the root file falls behind and both the `sharedConstants` version entry in
8	// .claudinite-checks.json and `cer/version-sync` go BLOCKING.
9	//
10	// WHICH FILE CARRIES IT MOVED with the chrome-extension pack's release-model
11	// overhaul (2026-08-21): the only automated, unattended version-write left in
12	// the pipeline is the deliberate minor/major dispatch
13	// (`chrome-extension-bump-version.yml`) — the routine patch bump that used to
14	// run inside the daily workflow's own `bump` job now belongs to the PR that
15	// touches a shipped file (`cer/version-bumped`), with a human in the loop who
16	// `cer/version-sync` will stop just as loudly if they forget the root file by
17	// hand. `chrome-extension-daily-release.yml` no longer bumps anything at all —
18	// it only checks whether the version already on `main` has shipped — so it is
19	// safe to take as a pure, un-diverged stub copy again.
20	//
21	// The delta is fragile in a specific, repeating way: the pack's
22	// `chrome-release-vendoring` migration MATERIALIZES this path — an unconditional
23	// verbatim overwrite from the stub, with no per-repo exemption seam (unlike a
24	// check finding, which .claudinite-checks.json can `accept`). Baselining
25	// re-attempts that write every cycle, so any agent that lands the withheld file
26	// mechanically deletes the step and silently re-opens the drift #241 closed.
27	// Issue #245 is the open decision on the real fix (teach release.config the root
28	// file, or give materialize an extension point); until it lands, this check is
29	// what makes the deletion loud instead of silent. When #245 resolves, delete
30	// this rule with the step.
31	//
32	// It keys on the BEHAVIOUR, not the step's label: the align step is the only
33	// place the workflow names the repo-root `package.json` as a literal file, since
34	// the stub reaches the two release-config paths through
35	// `${{ steps.cfg.outputs.* }}` only. So renaming or rewording the step keeps
36	// this silent, and only actually dropping the root-file write fires it.
37	const WORKFLOW = '.github/workflows/chrome-extension-bump-version.yml';
38	
39	// The quoted literal the align step's inline node script reads and writes.
40	const ROOT_PACKAGE_JSON = /(["'])package\.json\1/;
41	
42	const rule = {
43	  id: 'tldr/release-root-version-align',
44	  severity: 'blocking',
45	  description: "The daily-release workflow must keep aligning the repo-root package.json to the bumped version — it is this repo's local delta over the vendored stub",
46	  doc: '.claudinite/local/packs/tldr/RULES.md',
47	  scope: 'world',
48	  why: 'the release config bumps only the manifest and extension package.json, so without this step the repo-root package.json falls behind after every daily release and the version sharedConstants entry plus cer/version-sync both go BLOCKING (#241, #245)',
49	
50	  run(ctx) {
51	    const text = ctx.read(WORKFLOW);
52	    // A missing file is `cer/release-workflows`'s finding, not this one.
53	    if (text === null) return [];
54	    if (ROOT_PACKAGE_JSON.test(text)) return [];
55	
56	    return [finding(rule, {
57	      file: WORKFLOW,
58	      what: 'the bump job no longer writes the repo-root package.json — the "Align the root package.json to the bumped version" step is gone, so the next daily release will bump only the two release-config paths',
59	      fix: `restore the step from commit 2529b63 (PR #241) — it replaces the single \`"version": "X.Y.Z"\` token in the root package.json with \`steps.bump.outputs.version\` before the push. If it vanished after a baselining cycle, the chrome-release-vendoring materialize overwrote this file with the canon stub: re-apply the step rather than accepting the stub, and say so on #245`,
60	    })];
61	  },
62	};
63
