1	# Evaluating and routing a new item
2	
3	The shared method for three decisions every proposed addition to this corpus must pass through: **is it worthy** of inclusion at all, **which mechanism** should carry it, and — only for prose — **where does it go**. Any routine or person that adds an item — the [growth promote stage](tasks/growth-promote/task.md), an owner-requested retrospective pass, a hand edit — applies this same protocol, so the decision-making lives here once instead of being re-derived per caller.
4	
5	This is a Claudinite-internal doc used by the growth lifecycle (see [the canon-curation README](README.md)): it is **not** part of the mounted corpus and consuming repos do not `@import` it.
6	
7	An "item" is one **distilled, portable rule** — not a transcript, not a narration of what happened. A candidate still phrased as "here's what we did" has not been distilled yet and is below the bar on form alone, before any of the tests below. This doc picks up once a distilled rule exists and decides its fate.
8	
9	## Worthiness — does it earn a place at all
10	
11	The corpus is read read-only by every consuming repo, so a **duplicative** item (already covered) or an **undistilled** one (a story or a truism, not a rule) pollutes shared canon and costs every future reader. The bar guards against *those* — it is **not** a bar on *scope*: an item useful to only one project today can still earn a place (see Portable). Admit an item only when **all** hold:
12	
13	- **Distilled.** It is a single tight rule in the imperative, not a story, a log, or a restatement of a generic truism.
14	- **Portable — would a *future* project benefit?** Not "useful to every project today." An item can help only **one** project right now and still belong here, so long as another project — **especially one with a similar tech stack or process** — would benefit when it arrives. Being specific to a technology or a process is **not** disqualifying: generalize it and route it to that technology's or practice's home. What disqualifies is leaning on *this* project's non-transferable particulars — a product requirement, or a one-off incident in how it happened to call some API. The test, a genuinely hard one: *if another project with a similar tech stack came along, would it benefit from this?* Yes → portable; only-ever-this-product → local. A rule mined from Claudinite's own test suite is the hardest case: it reads as generic testing craft even when it actually depends on Claudinite's own shape — the only project whose tests build git-repo fixtures because its checks take a repo as input. Before promoting one, grep the fleet's own callers of the pattern the rule is about; zero callers outside this project's own conformance tests means the lesson is local however general its wording (#857: a fixture-signing rule read as portable, was promoted to `writing-tests`, then reverted once every caller of the fixture helper turned out to be a Claudinite conformance test).
15	- **Durable and reusable.** It will still apply on a future, unseen task — not a one-off, not a situational detail, not something already implied by an existing rule.
16	- **Readable through the channel it lands in.** A rule whose premise is that the delivery channel
17	  itself failed cannot be carried by that channel. Promote #497 admitted "the tell that the SessionStart
18	  hook did not fire" as pack prose — and pack prose is what that hook delivers, so in the one situation
19	  the rule describes it is not in context to be read. Detecting a channel's own failure belongs in code,
20	  not in the payload the channel carries; reject such an item here rather than rewording it.
21	- **Not already covered.** The insight does not already exist **anywhere** in the corpus, even worded differently or owned by a different file. This is checked against the *entire* corpus, not just the file it would land in — see [Dedupe against the whole corpus](#dedupe-against-the-whole-corpus).
22	
23	Reject on any miss — but the misses that matter are *undistilled*, *already-covered*, or *genuinely one-off*, not merely *narrow*. When you're torn over a real, non-duplicate rule, lean toward **keeping** it — the goal is a broad library. When you're torn over whether something is a duplicate, or a rule at all, leave it out. The failure to avoid is padding the canon with restatements of what's already there; admitting a narrow-but-reusable rule is not that failure.
24	
25	### Dedupe against the whole corpus
26	
27	Before admitting anything, read across the corpus, not only the file you expect to own the item. The same insight is frequently already present under a different heading or in an adjacent group. If it sharpens an **existing** rule, fold it in with a minimal edit rather than adding a second bullet that says nearly the same thing — and never weaken or restate what is already there in the process.
28	
29	**Sweep last, and case-insensitively.** A dedupe pass is only evidence about the text it actually read, so it runs **after** every re-home, merge and edit the change makes — a sweep run early and never re-run reports clean on content that has since moved under it. Measured on #740 (the seven-PR promote consolidation): the sweep ran *before* two lessons were re-homed out of a folded-away skill file into `packs/basics/RULES.md`, and **three** copies of the same unknown-state rule reached the owner, who found them by reading. The re-run then surfaced a further pair the pattern had missed because it was case-sensitive and the survivors were capitalised. So: sweep as the last step, match case-insensitively, and state the similarity threshold you swept at so the "no remaining near-duplicates" claim is checkable.
30	
31	## Mechanism triage — prose is the fallback, not the default
32	
33	A worthy item next descends the **promotion ladder** ([../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md) owns it): platform setting (always paired with its verifying check) → PreToolUse hook → conformance check → skill → prose. The *first* rung that can carry the item wins — a rule about repo state becomes a check whose failure message *is* the lesson; a bad action to prevent becomes a guard; a procedure or knowledge with a nameable trigger becomes (or joins) a skill. Only an item none of those can carry — judgment, in-flight behavior, signature-less knowledge — proceeds to the file routing below, and its landing **names that reason** in the promote log so conversion rates stay auditable.
34	
35	**"No universal signature" alone never routes an item to prose.** A rule converts to a check when a *narrow, file-scoped* signature covers the **grounded cases** — the concrete shapes the rule was distilled from — even though no signature covers every conceivable violation. Gate it relevance-first so it stays inert off-target, and document the genuinely signature-less residue in the rule's own comments as out of scope. The prose rung is only for an item whose grounded cases *themselves* have no reliable signature (pure judgment, runtime/in-flight behavior).
36	
37	## Routing — picking the right file (rung-5 items only)
38	
39	Routing is robust when it keys on **stable file groups**, not on the current roster of individual files (which grows over time). The corpus is organized into a few groups, each with its own selection rule:
40	
41	1. **The practice group** — durable, project-agnostic practices, each file a self-contained, reusable unit of know-how the agent applies whenever its subject comes up (engineering, agentic, git/GitHub, testing, investigation, discipline, architecture), partitioned **by kind of practice** with each file owning one recurring subject cluster. This group spans **two folders that differ only by *when* the rule loads**: `always/` for a rule that applies to essentially every task (the index `@`-imports it, so it's force-loaded every session), and `tasks/` for a subject-gated rule read on demand when its trigger fires. Route in two steps: first match the item's *kind* to the file whose cluster already owns that subject; then keep it in `always/` only if it genuinely isn't tied to one kind of task (the rare case — `always/` stays small), otherwise it belongs in `tasks/`. Read the group's own index (the root `CLAUDE.md`) to find the current owner for a kind — never from memory, since the set of clusters can grow.
42	2. **The per-user group** — interaction preferences and trigger phrases. This group does **not live in this repo**: an item of this kind routes out to the person it belongs to, never into the practice group and never back into the canon.
43	3. **The per-technology group** — practices specific to one technology, **one file per technology**. Route a technology-specific item to that technology's file. When **no pack homes that technology** (not even a stub), the item doesn't land in a loose doc — it **mints a fingerprinted stub pack** (a `packs/<tech>/`, delivered in its own PR), so the next project on that stack self-declares it; [promote](tasks/growth-promote/task.md)'s stub-minting floor and [the generate-project-instructions skill](../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/skills/generate-project-instructions/SKILL.md) own the mechanics.
44	
45	Pick **exactly one** owner. If an item plausibly fits two files, choose the single best one — never split one item across files, and never duplicate it into both. The group decides the *axis* (kind, person, or technology); the file within the group is then the one whose existing scope the item falls squarely inside.
46	
47	### When nothing fits
48	
49	An item that matches **no** existing file is **not** a reject signal by itself — a genuinely new category of lesson is meant to be learnable, so a worthy item that no file owns earns its own file. Resolve it in this order:
50	
51	- **Route into an existing owner** when one genuinely fits — the first choice. If the item belongs to a file's cluster and merely sits slightly off-center, a small stretch toward that owner beats spinning up a new file. A new file is for when no existing file's scope genuinely fits, **not** a way to dodge folding into an existing owner.
52	- **Open a new file** when the item clears the [Worthiness](#worthiness--does-it-earn-a-place-at-all) bar in full — distilled, portable, durable and reusable, and not already covered anywhere in the corpus — **and** no existing file's scope genuinely fits it. That is the whole bar: nothing more is required. Do **not** also demand that you expect the cluster to recur, that forcing the item into the closest file would *distort* it, or default to rejecting when the new-file call is a close one — those extra hurdles are dropped. Creating a file obliges registering it where the corpus is indexed and in any routing table, in the **same** change, so it never lands orphaned (see [Keep the write surface bounded](#keep-the-write-surface-bounded)).
53	
54	The loosening above is **only** to the new-cluster hurdle, never to the per-item bar. An item that misses [Worthiness](#worthiness--does-it-earn-a-place-at-all) — a one-off, non-portable or project-specific, a restatement of a generic truism, or already covered anywhere in the corpus — is rejected whether or not a file already exists for it; for the per-item admission decision, the default-to-reject-when-unsure tiebreak still stands.
55	
56	## Keep the write surface bounded
57	
58	Once worthiness and routing are settled, the edit touches **only** the single owning file: add or sharpen one terse rule in that file's existing voice and format, and change nothing else. Do not "improve" unrelated rules while you are in there. The sole exception is the new-file path above, whose surface is itself bounded to the new file plus its index and routing-table registration.
59

1	# EdFringeNow — the data pipeline (scraper/ and data/)
2	
3	The domain of this pack: getting show data out of edfringe.com and into the
4	committed files the site serves. Read it before touching `scraper/` or anything
5	under `data/`. The API's own field reference lives in
6	[scraper/SCRAPING.md](../../../../scraper/SCRAPING.md) and the file layout in
7	[scraper/README.md](../../../../scraper/README.md) — this is the working
8	judgment those two don't carry.
9	
10	## The live API is unreachable from a session — don't try, and don't fake it
11	
12	`edfringe-tikketr-web-api.equhost.com` is blocked by the sandbox egress proxy
13	(403 at the CONNECT). So: no session — this one included —
14	can verify a scraper change against live data. Anything that must touch the API
15	runs through a sanctioned workflow: the `Scrape edfringe shows (full)` workflow
16	(`.github/workflows/scrape.yml`), `Fetch ticket prices (one-off)`
17	(`prices.yml`), or the `refresh-shows` / `refresh-tickets` scheduled tasks.
18	Never "verify" a scraper change by reasoning about what the API probably
19	returns — either have a sanctioned workflow run it, or say plainly that it is
20	unverified.
21	
22	For one-off API questions (a field's shape, an enum's value set, whether an
23	operation exists at all), `scraper/SCRAPING.md` is the reference. When it falls
24	short there is one legitimate source short of asking the owner:
25	**`www.edfringe.com` itself is reachable**, and its Next.js bundles carry the
26	client's complete GraphQL operation set — every query, mutation and fragment,
27	with full field selections. Recipe in SCRAPING.md ("Reaching it from a Claude
28	Code web session"). That is reading a public asset from an allowed host, and it
29	is how the "no bulk price endpoint" claim was finally settled. It tells you what
30	a query would look like, never what it returns — so a change checked only that
31	way is still unverified against live data and must be reported as such. If that
32	doesn't answer it either, ask the repo owner rather than building a bypass.
33	
34	`python3 scraper/normalize.py --selftest` is the one transform check that runs
35	offline; it exercises raw→master→day-file→`shows.min.json` on a fixture, so a
36	normalizer change is verifiable here even though a fetch change is not. Because
37	it is the only offline verification a scraper change can get, it must stay wired
38	into `scripts/verify.sh` — the `edfringe-normalizer-selftest-in-verify` check
39	enforces that (a step *label* naming the self-test does not count; only a command
40	line does).
41	
42	## `ticketStatus`, never the `soldOut` boolean
43	
44	"Can I get a ticket" comes from the per-performance `ticketStatus`, not the
45	`soldOut` flag: a performance can be `soldOut: false` and still have nothing to
46	sell online (`NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE`). The site treats `SOLD_OUT` and
47	`NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE` as unavailable and everything else as available
48	(`NO_TICKETS_STATUSES` in `js/app.js`), and unknown means available. Any new
49	availability logic — client or scraper — keys off `ticketStatus`; `soldOut` is
50	carried through for display only.
51	
52	## A price belongs to a performance, not to a show
53	
54	The same run sells at several prices: previews cheaper than the main run,
55	weekends dearer than weekdays. The first price pass didn't know that — it
56	called `performancePrices` for **one** performance per show and filed the answer
57	under the show. Pre-festival the performance it picked was almost always the
58	earliest, i.e. a preview, so **1,016 of 3,664 priced shows (28%) published their
59	cheapest night as their price**: Alfie Brown's £15/£16 run shipped as £8.50.
60	
61	The fix is not a rule about previews, and adding a "skip previews" or
62	"price after date X" heuristic re-creates the same class of bug from a different
63	angle — it still picks one performance and hopes it represents the rest.
64	**Price every performance.** There is no bulk price *field*, but GraphQL aliases
65	make one request carry a whole show's run (`fetch_prices.prices_query`), so full
66	per-night pricing costs roughly the same ~3,700 requests as the old pass. There
67	is no call budget to economise against here, so don't design as if there were.
68	
69	Which payload gets which number is the load-bearing distinction:
70	
71	| payload | question it answers | price |
72	|---|---|---|
73	| master, `shows.min.json` (planner) | what does this *show* cost? | run-wide `priceMin`..`priceMax` |
74	| `data/days/*.json` (Now page) | what does it cost *tonight*? | that performance's own `pm` |
75	
76	A performance the cache has no entry for gets **no `pm` at all** — "Price TBC" —
77	rather than the show's minimum. Borrowing a neighbouring night's figure is
78	exactly the bug above, and a lower bound presented as the price is a lie about
79	money even when every number in it is real.
80	
81	## Prices are fetched once, and "unknown" is a third state the encoding must keep
82	
83	`data/prices.json` is a fetch-once cache (`scraper/fetch_prices.py`), off the
84	nightly path: a show's price bands are set when it goes on sale, unlike its
85	ticket status. `refresh-shows` reads the cache and carries the amounts through
86	untouched — it never re-fetches them. So the festival keeps adding shows the
87	cache has never seen, and **a show with no price is a normal, permanent state of
88	the data**, not a gap the pipeline should close.
89	
90	The cache carries two entry shapes and both must stay readable: current entries
91	have `sets` + `perfs` (per performance), and entries from the old pass have a
92	bare whole-show `min`/`max`. The migration completes one show per re-run, so
93	dropping the legacy shape — or emptying the cache to "start clean" — would blank
94	every price on the site until a full pass finished. `price_sets` reads both.
95	
96	Which means the encoding carries three states, not two, and every stage has to
97	preserve the distinction:
98	
99	| state | master | wire |
100	|---|---|---|
101	| costs nothing | `priceMin: 0` | `pm: 0` |
102	| priced | `priceMin: 22.5` | `pm: 22.5` |
103	| unknown | `priceMin: null` | no `pm` key at all |
104	
105	`priceMin: 0` and `free: true` are **not** the same claim and don't always agree.
106	The flag comes from the listing; the £0 can also come from the price API, which
107	returns a single `Price band 1` at £0.00 for a handful of shows the listing
108	doesn't flag free — pay-what-you-want, or a box office that never set a price
109	(10 of 3,664 in the first full run). Both readings are honest about what a ticket
110	costs, so the price path keys off `priceMin`, and `free` stays what the *listing*
111	said. Don't "fix" one to match the other.
112	
113	Never encode unknown as `0`, and never let a decoder default it to one: a stage
114	that collapses three states into two is lying about money, and nothing
115	downstream can recover the difference. What the site then *does* with an unknown
116	price is a product decision, not a pipeline one — it lives in `shared/price.js`.
117	
118	Two traps in the raw price payload, both already handled and both worth not
119	re-introducing: amounts arrive as **strings**, and nearly every show carries a
120	£0.00 "Personal Assistant" concession (a carer's companion ticket) that must not
121	be read as the cheapest price. See the pricing section of
122	[scraper/SCRAPING.md](../../../../scraper/SCRAPING.md).
123	
124	## The API stamps performances in UTC — cross the zone once, at the edge
125	
126	The listing API's `dateTime` is a real UTC instant (`"2026-08-06T11:45:00.000Z"`),
127	**not** Edinburgh wall-clock with a decorative `Z`. Slicing the digits out of that
128	string is the trap: it looks like it works — every date and time in it is
129	plausible — and in August it is silently an hour wrong for the whole catalogue.
130	That is exactly what shipped, and what #275 cost to undo: 60,115 performances
131	listed an hour early, with the tell being shows that name their own time (a 10am
132	"Shakespeare for Breakfast" sitting at 09:00).
133	
134	The pipeline has **one** time-zone crossing, and it is `normalize.local_date_start`.
135	`refresh_ticket_status.py` and `fetch_prices.py` share it so a performance is keyed
136	by the same local date and start everywhere. Everything written after it — the
137	master, `data/days/*.json`, `availability.min.json`, `shows.min.json` — is already
138	Edinburgh wall-clock, so **no stage downstream parses, converts, or re-offsets a
139	time**. Treating a stored value as UTC a second time is the same bug from the other
140	end.
141	
142	Two consequences to hold on to when touching this:
143	
144	- **A "now" compared against these times is read in Edinburgh too** — `js/clock.js`
145	  (`festivalNow` / `festivalDate`), never the device clock. A UK visitor cannot see
146	  the difference, which is why a device clock survives review; a visitor planning
147	  from another zone reintroduces the whole drift.
148	- **A conversion change is a full-snapshot change.** The committed data is generator
149	  output, so the fix is not complete until the master is rebuilt through the new
150	  conversion and every derived artifact regenerated from it. Shifting the boundary
151	  moves performances between day files (two late 31 Aug performances now fall into
152	  1 Sep, outside the August day files, and live only in the master and the planner's
153	  catalogue) — expect that and check it, rather than reading it as data loss.
154	
155	## Two client-cached files joined by key need a fingerprint, or a generation split breaks the join
156	
157	`shows.min.json` (catalogue) and `availability.min.json` (ticket-status
158	sidecar) are cached independently in the browser and joined client-side by
159	performance key (venue + date + time). The UTC time-shift fix (`c1bc2a6`,
160	above) moved every one of those keys by an hour — a browser still holding the
161	pre-fix sidecar cached alongside a post-fix catalogue joined at 6.2%
162	(3,751/60,115) instead of 100%, rendering every planner favourite "No dates."
163	even though both files were individually correct (#309). A per-file TTL has
164	no way to detect that two files it's serving came from incompatible backend
165	generations.
166	
167	The fix is `join_fingerprint(master)` in `scraper/normalize.py`, mirrored
168	exactly as `joinFingerprint()` in `plan/lib/hydrate.js` (same algorithm in
169	both languages — `normalize.py`'s self-test asserts they agree, and that a
170	moved start time changes the fingerprint while a price change doesn't),
171	carried as the sidecar's `k` field. `plan/plan.js` compares its own
172	`joinFingerprint()` of the catalogue it holds against the sidecar's `k` and
173	calls `evictCached()` on both URLs on a mismatch, forcing a refetch of the
174	matching pair. Any future backend change that moves a performance's join key
175	needs this same fingerprint-and-evict shape — a plain TTL bump doesn't cover
176	it, because both files can be individually "fresh enough" by TTL and still
177	belong to different generations.
178	
179	## The committed data is generated output — regenerate it, never hand-edit it
180	
181	`data/raw_pages/` is a git-ignored regenerable cache. `data/normalized/`,
182	`data/venues.json` and `data/days/` **are** committed, because the browser
183	fetches them — but they are still generator output. Fix the data by fixing
184	`scraper/normalize.py` and re-running it (`--merge` for a top-up, no flag for a
185	full rebuild from the raw cache); a hand-edit is silently overwritten by the next
186	`refresh-shows` run and leaves the bug in the generator.
187	
188	`data/prices.json` is the one exception, and it is an exception to the *direction*
189	rather than the rule: it is committed, but it is normalize.py's **input**, written
190	by `scraper/fetch_prices.py`. Nothing regenerates it on a schedule, so nothing
191	overwrites a hand-edit either — which is precisely why editing it by hand is still
192	wrong: the edit survives, silently disagreeing with the box office forever. Re-run
193	the fetch. The `edfringe-data-dir-is-generator-output` check allows it **by name**,
194	so a second file can't ride in on its shape.
195	
196	## A long-running workflow that commits generated data will race the hourly refresh
197	
198	Any workflow that writes to `data/normalized/`, `data/venues.json` or `data/days/`
199	and can run for more than about an hour is racing `refresh-tickets`, which pushes
200	to `main` every hour through the festival. A plain `git push` at the end of such a
201	run is not occasionally rejected — it is *guaranteed* to be, so the commit step has
202	to expect it. `#292` lost a full 2h39m price-fetch pass this way: the commit
203	existed only on the runner, and by the time it tried to push, `main` had moved.
204	
205	Recovery has to **re-derive, not merge** — every contested file is generator
206	output from both writers, so a rebase would conflict on generated bytes whose only
207	correct value is "whatever the generator says now," not either side's stored
208	version. `prices.yml`'s commit step (`.github/workflows/prices.yml`, the retry
209	loop in its "Commit prices and regenerated data" step) is the worked fix: on a
210	rejected push, fetch `origin/main`, take its generated files, regenerate from that
211	master plus this workflow's own non-generated input, retry. A new long-running
212	workflow that writes these paths needs the same shape from the start, not a
213	bespoke recovery discovered the same way after the fact.
214	
215	## Changing the wire format is a four-file change
216	
217	The day files and `shows.min.json` reference `data/venues.json`'s global lists
218	**by position** (`genre`, `room`, `subs`, `ts`; `g`, `rm`, `sg`, `ar`). That
219	encoding has one producer and two decoders, and they must move together:
220	
221	- producer — `scraper/normalize.py` (`build_lookups` / `build_day_files` /
222	  `minify_master` / `build_availability`)
223	- decoder 1 — `js/app.js` `adaptShow`, for the day files
224	- decoder 2 — `plan/lib/hydrate.js` `rehydrateShows`, the exact inverse of
225	  `minify_master`, round-tripped against the real committed files by
226	  `plan/lib/__tests__/hydrate.test.mjs`
227	
228	Add or drop an indexed field and all three change in the same commit. That the
229	indices still *resolve* is enforced by the `edfringe-lookup-indices` check — it
230	catches a lookup list regenerated without its day files, but nothing can catch a
231	decoder left reading the old key, so check both decoders by hand.
232	
233	Two properties of that encoding are load-bearing for caching, and both fail
234	silently:
235	
236	- **The lookup lists are append-only** (`extend_lookup`). The browser holds
237	  `shows.min.json` for four days and `venues.json` for one, so a stale catalogue
238	  is routinely decoded against a newer lookup file. An entry that changed index
239	  would relabel shows' genres and rooms with no error anywhere. Entries are never
240	  dropped, even once the master stops using them.
241	- **`shows.min.json` carries nothing that changes through the day.** Ticket
242	  status lives in `availability.min.json` (its own status list, indexing into
243	  nothing, so `refresh-tickets` can rewrite it alone). Putting a status back in
244	  the catalogue would tie that bulky download to the ticket refresh *and*
245	  freeze availability for anyone holding a cached copy — the bug in #249,
246	  re-created from the other end.
247	  `hydrate.test.mjs` asserts each wire performance carries only `d` and `s`.
248	
249	The same three-way move applies to plain (non-indexed) wire keys such as the
250	price fields `pm` / `px`, with one extra hazard: the round-trip test compares the
251	rehydrated record to the master **as JSON**, so a new master key has to appear in
252	the *same position* in `normalize_event`'s dict and in `rehydrateShows`'s object
253	literal. Adding it in one place and appending it in the other fails the
254	round-trip on key order alone, which reads as a data bug and isn't one.
255

1	# edfringe-requirements — the executable-requirements harness here
2	
3	How this repo runs its spec (`product/requirements.md`) as tests. The framework
4	conventions are the `executable-requirements` pack; the judgment layer is
5	`spec-driven-product` + the `writing-tests` skill. This pack carries only what
6	those don't: the mechanics of a **real-headless-browser** golden harness (the
7	canon's worked examples render with satori/jsdom or Flutter — this repo is the
8	first Playwright port) and the local approval/fixture policy. Layout, lanes and
9	commands live in [product/requirements/README.md](../../../../product/requirements/README.md)
10	— don't restate them; this file is the judgment and the traps.
11	
12	## The document reads as pictures
13	
14	- `product/requirements.md` is scanned by sight: under each visual leaf its
15	  golden is **visible, uncollapsed**; every textual expansion (acceptance
16	  notes, proof pointers) is **collapsed** in a `<details>` block. An optimal
17	  requirements document has almost no words on the page.
18	- **A visual leaf's statement is a line, not a paragraph.** The golden already
19	  carries the exact copy, counts, colours and placement — restating them in
20	  prose only competes with the picture. Say what is being asserted; let the
21	  image say how it looks. Anything genuinely not visible (a threshold, a rule
22	  behind the state, a condition that produced it) goes in a collapsed
23	  **Notes** block, never in the statement.
24	- **A golden is the smallest surface that proves its leaf** — an element crop,
25	  a clipped region, or a stitched composite (e.g. one grid lane narrowed to a
26	  few days, recomposed with its label and verdict columns, no header) — never
27	  the whole page or even the whole control. The capture recipe lives on the
28	  case (`capture: "<selector>"` or `capture(page, tools)`; see
29	  `shared/capture-tools.js`); whole-page capture is a deliberate exception,
30	  not a default. Scoping is judgment: crop to what the leaf asserts, keep just
31	  enough surroundings to orient.
32	- **A change over time is an animation, not a coded assertion.** When a
33	  requirement is about what an action *changes* — a dismissal that sticks, a
34	  pick that swaps one card for another — capture the same region before and
35	  after (and after a reload, where persistence is the point) and play the
36	  frames as one animated golden (`tools.animate`). A flow is shown as a flow.
37	  Reserve `stitchV`/`stitchH` for things that are genuinely side by side rather
38	  than sequential.
39	- **An animated golden is an APNG, never a GIF.** It animates in GitHub
40	  markdown exactly like a GIF. The encoder is `shared/png.js`'s
41	  `encodeAnimated`; the comparator detects an animated golden and compares
42	  bytes only, since a pixel differ reads one still frame and would describe
43	  the wrong thing.
44	
45	## A requirement is a feature, not a module
46	
47	The spec is organised by what the product *does*, never by how the code is
48	arranged. "Shared code" is not a requirement category: a rule both front-ends
49	follow is one feature, and its picture shows **both** the Now page and the
50	planner — a rule only half the site follows is not the feature. Those
51	cross-page features sit in their own part **after** the two page-by-page
52	segments, so each page reads as a whole first.
53	
54	Cross-page proof is ordinary: a case may navigate between the pages (or open a
55	second page, when something fixed at context creation — a device timezone —
56	has to differ) and stitch or animate the surfaces into one golden.
57	
58	## Prefer several pictures over one coded leaf
59	
60	Before routing a leaf to `behavior` or `logic`, ask whether it **decomposes
61	into observable states**. A statement joined by "and" usually does, and each
62	part is then its own numbered sub-leaf with its own picture — the parent
63	becomes a heading. The time wheel went this way: "5-minute steps, opens at
64	now + 2 h, ends at 29:55" was one coded leaf and is now `3.7.1`–`3.7.3`, three
65	crops anyone can check by eye. Sub-leaves are cheap; a coded assertion the
66	owner has to read code to trust is not.
67	
68	Reserve the coded kinds for what genuinely has no picture:
69	
70	- **`behavior`** — a gesture's outgoing consequence (a URL built, bytes
71	  downloaded, storage written), or a fact the OS paints rather than the page
72	  (a native `title` tooltip, a cursor — neither can appear in a screenshot).
73	- **`logic`** — a pure rule with no rendered surface at all. When the rule is
74	  about *how values are written*, prefer a **table** over prose: a case may
75	  declare `table: { columns, rows }`, the gallery renders it into the spec, and
76	  its `verify()` proves every row against the shipped code — so the table a
77	  reader sees is generated evidence, not a hand-typed claim.
78	
79	When a leaf lands in a coded kind *because* the product makes it invisible,
80	say so in its Notes and name what product change would make it visual — that
81	is a real finding about the UI, not just a testing limitation.
82	
83	## The browser is part of the expected
84	
85	- A golden is only comparable under the **exact Chromium that rendered it**.
86	  The harness pins the Playwright version and refuses any other
87	  (`shared/harness/browser.js`); CI installs that pin per run, the Claude
88	  sandbox ships it globally. **Bumping the pin re-renders every golden** — it
89	  is a re-baselining, done deliberately and approved like one, never a drive-by
90	  upgrade.
91	- When the comparison ever flaps, the fix is **more determinism, not a
92	  tolerance**: the comparator stays at zero diff. The determinism levers are
93	  all in one place (the harness): fixed clock via `page.clock`, fixed
94	  geolocation, seeded `Math.random`, route-fulfilled network, frozen
95	  animations, `--font-render-hinting=none --force-color-profile=srgb`.
96	
97	## Traps this harness already paid for (don't re-derive)
98	
99	- **Geolocation exists only on secure origins.** The fake origin is `https://`
100	  — route interception fulfils before any TLS, so no certificate is involved.
101	  On plain http the app silently keeps its built-in simulated clock and the
102	  whole render lands on the wrong day.
103	- **The app adopts the device clock only on an in-UK geolocation fix** — the
104	  harness's fixed location is central Edinburgh precisely so the pinned clock
105	  is what renders; deny geolocation (or move abroad) and you are rendering the
106	  app's own pre-set simulated moment instead, a different day file entirely.
107	- **A CSS freeze does not stop Web-Animations-API animations.** The planner's
108	  FLIP board diff runs through `element.animate` — the harness stubs it to
109	  land on end states; without the stub, captures race the animation.
110	- **Fonts arrive via the Google Fonts CSS URL**, so the vendored `fonts.css`'s
111	  `url(/__vendor/…)` references resolve against `fonts.googleapis.com` — the
112	  vendor route must match on path, host-agnostic, or every glyph silently
113	  falls back and all text shifts by a pixel.
114	- **Vendoring the web fonts is only half the font problem.** Every character
115	  they don't carry — an emoji, `▾`, `≤`, a Cyrillic show title — is drawn from
116	  the fonts *installed on the machine*, so the goldens quietly become a record
117	  of the renderer's font set. It cost a red CI lane: the walk-time line
118	  (`🚶 5 min · £16`) measured wider on the GitHub runner, wrapped, and every
119	  show card came out 21px taller. The harness now launches Chromium under a
120	  generated `FONTCONFIG_FILE` whose only font directory is
121	  `harness/vendor/systemfonts/` — the host's fonts cannot reach the page. A new
122	  emoji or script in the product or the fixtures needs that subset rebuilt
123	  (see the folder's README), or it renders as tofu.
124	- **Reproducing a golden-flake locally: use the harness's own pixel comparator
125	  (`compare.js`), not a raw byte/hash compare.** On 2026-08-11 (#335) a first
126	  repro script hashed the rendered PNG's bytes across repeated cold renders
127	  and found a hash difference — looked like a reproduction of the flake, but
128	  `compare.js` (pixelmatch, zero tolerated diff) passed the identical images
129	  at 0 pixels differing. A byte-hash compare is strictly tighter than what CI
130	  actually enforces (bit-exact *pixels*, not encoder bytes), so it manufactures
131	  false positives; the real comparator is what settles whether a flake is real.
132	- **A red CI lane's diff image is unreachable from a session — reproduce it
133	  locally.** `ui-requirements` uploads a `requirements-failure-artifacts`
134	  artifact, but `download_workflow_run_artifact` hands back a
135	  `*.blob.core.windows.net` URL and the egress proxy denies it at CONNECT
136	  (`curl: (56) CONNECT tunnel failed, response 403`). On 2026-08-11 a session
137	  burned the download and then came back ~4.5 minutes later to re-probe the
138	  proxy for the same image; the golden it was chasing ended the session
139	  undiagnosed. Use `get_job_logs` with a large `tail_lines` to learn *which*
140	  case failed, then re-run that case locally — `npm run test:ui` writes the
141	  `.actual.png` / `.diff.png` into `shared/.artifacts/` itself.
142	- **A floating popup dies under a full-page screenshot** (the capture scrolls,
143	  and scroll dismisses tips/legends/optimizer pops). A popup-state case sets
144	  `viewportOnly: true` and captures the viewport crop.
145	- **"Ready" is not `networkidle`.** The pages settle their async work into
146	  observable state — the footer version popup's text, the search placeholder's
147	  show count. Wait on those (`case-helpers.js`), plus `document.fonts.ready`.
148	- **Hover-driven UI must be opened inside `capture()`, not `drive()`.** The
149	  runner settles the scroll between the two, and scrolling moves an element out
150	  from under the pointer — which fires `mouseleave` and closes anything the
151	  hover opened. That is correct product behaviour; the capture just has to
152	  happen on the right side of it.
153	
154	## The fixture freeze
155	
156	- `shared/fixtures/data/` is a snapshot of the **real committed data**, cast by
157	  the committed builder for state variety (sold-out / free / price-unknown /
158	  tight / every planner verdict). It is **frozen**: the nightly data refresh
159	  never touches it, and no case may reach for `data/` live files.
160	- Every deviation from the source bytes is documented as an `ADJUST` in the
161	  builder — a fixture edit without one is hand-invented data.
162	- Re-running the builder re-casts every golden. That is a re-baselining: run it
163	  only with the owner's approval, and land builder + fixtures + goldens +
164	  gallery in one reviewed change.
165	
166	## Golden approval, concretely
167	
168	- Surface the committed golden alongside `shared/.artifacts/<case>.actual.png`
169	  and `.diff.png`, and ask the owner (AskUserQuestion popup, per-item, per the
170	  owner's preferences).
171	- Say so in the PR body — the goldens are the review surface.
172	- An intended UI change lands as: spec edit (doc-first, red) → implementation →
173	  `npm run refresh:ui` → the refreshed PNGs ride the same diff.

1	# Growth — promote lessons into the canon (the central stage)
2	
3	The [growth lifecycle](../../README.md)'s central stage: read the target members' local packs, lift the portable lessons into the shared canon, and open a PR against the canon's default branch **for the owner to approve**. Declared only by the Claudinite home repo, so it runs **once, centrally**, never per project.
4	
5	The run's **Context section is binding scope**: it names the exact target members (those whose local packs changed in the window). Work exactly that list — the fleet enumeration already happened in the precondition; **do not enumerate the fleet yourself or widen past the Context**.
6	
7	Promotion is the **judgment gate before shared canon**. This run opens a PR and **never arms auto-merge** — the owner approves it. But don't lean on that review as the portability check: [extract](../../../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/tasks/growth-extract/task.md) stays project-specific by design, so it's no second opinion, and the owner can't re-derive every portability call. This task's judgment is the real thing between a bad rule and every project that reads the canon — keep the bar high (dedupe against the whole corpus; default to reject when unsure).
8	
9	## Conventions used in this doc
10	
11	- **GitHub access is MCP-only** (`mcp__github__*`). You are outside each member repo — read its files over the API (get-file-contents, never a cross-repo checkout; the sandbox has no cross-repo git). The canon PR is opened over MCP too.
12	- **A member's local packs** are everything under `.claudinite/local/packs/` (the legacy `.claudinite/local_packs/` accepted during the rename window) — its own packs, never the read-only mounted canon elsewhere under `.claudinite/`.
13	- **`main`** stands for the canon's default branch.
14	
15	## What each run does
16	
17	### 1. Read the target members' local **packs**
18	
19	For each member named in Context, read its **local packs**. The candidate pool is a local pack's captured knowledge — its `RULES.md` **prose** AND its own **checks** (a `<pack>/*.mjs` rule module — its id, description, and failure message *are* a captured, enforceable lesson; the strongest promotion lifts it to a **canon check**, generalized, reusing the [prose-to-checks](../../../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/skills/prose-to-checks/SKILL.md) mechanics — or to canon prose when it doesn't generalize to a check). **Out of scope, staying put:** a lesson deliberately placed as a **code comment at its call site**, a project's task scripts, product source, and config. Never promote from product source. A genuinely portable rule that looks trapped in a code comment was mis-placed at extract time — leave it for a future extract pass to re-home into a pack. You don't need to tell new from old — the dedup step drops anything the canon already carries. No barrier holds tonight's extracts: read whatever is already **merged** on each member's default branch; anything landing mid-run is tomorrow's input.
20	
21	### 2. Generalize each candidate — *before* judging whether it belongs
22	
23	Generalize first, then decide worthiness — never the reverse. The act of generalizing is itself the portability probe — a rule that goes vacuous when lifted, or only makes sense with its project's context, isn't portable; leave it local. Work the rule standalone (origin naming and grouping carry no weight); strip the project (names, files, example stay in the origin repo — promote the distilled rule only); a **technology** mention isn't a disqualifier (lift it to the broadest scope that stays true — tech-specific is fine, *product*-specific is not); decide tool-vs-process and frame it for that home.
24	
25	### 3. Then judge worthiness — deduped against the *entire* corpus
26	
27	Holding the generalized rule, decide if it earns a place by the bar [item-routing.md](../../item-routing.md) owns (don't restate its gates). Lean **inclusive** — keep anything a future project could use — but be strict about **duplication**: dedupe against **every** corpus doc, not only the one you'd expect to own it.
28	
29	### 4. Triage the mechanism, then route
30	
31	- **Descend the promotion ladder first** ([item-routing.md](../../item-routing.md)'s mechanism triage). Prose is the fallback, not the default: a lesson a check can carry is **authored as the check** in this PR — the rule module in the right pack, the failure message carrying the generalized lesson, **plus a fixture test proving it fires** on a violating input and stays quiet on a clean one. When a confident detection-plus-fixture can't be authored unattended, land the lesson as prose **and** open a tagged conformance-backlog issue — never a silently-shipped broken check.
32	- **Route** each prose rule to its **one** owning doc ([item-routing.md](../../item-routing.md) owns the placement); match its voice and format; pick exactly one owner, never split or duplicate.
33	- **A technology with no home → mint a fingerprinted stub pack, in its own PR**, reusing the pack-writing mechanics [the generate-project-instructions skill](../../../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/skills/generate-project-instructions/SKILL.md) owns — `packs/<tech>/` with `pack.mjs` (add the `marker`/`detect` fingerprint when the technology carries a reliable one, else `detect: null`), a `RULES.md` seeded from the lesson, a `README.md`, and its `packs/README.md` index row. A minted pack ships in its **own** PR, split from the run's lesson-promotion PR (a new pack earns its own review surface). Never mint from imagination and never park an empty one to fill later — a pack minted here is populated from the *real, portable lesson* that justified it. Do not pad it with speculative rules no project earned — the "written from imagination, not distilled from worked examples" failure; an ungroundable rule isn't written. (Authoring a *fuller* pack from a technology's usage across the whole fleet — rather than a single lesson — is the per-repo pack-discovery task's job, not this floor's.) The follow-ups a fresh stub invites — enriching it from known best practices, triaging which skills it should require, spinning up dependent/aspect packs — are **not** automated here: note them for the owner and leave them to a later, deliberate pass.
34	- **Write it terse — when + what.** State the relevance (*when* it applies) and the rule (*what* to do); add a *why* only to flag severity, in a few words.
35	- **Bounded write surface — `packs/`/`skills/` only** (CI-enforced on the PR). Edit only the one owning doc — or, for a check-conversion, only the new rule module, its registration in the pack registry, and its fixture test. Don't "improve" unrelated rules while you're in there. The two bounded exceptions (both within `packs/`): the new-doc path [item-routing.md](../../item-routing.md) owns, and minting a stub pack.
36	- **Bump the `version` of every pack you edited** (`packs/<id>/pack.mjs`) — a pack's directory reaches a member only when that number exceeds the one the member has installed, so a promoted lesson left at the old version stays in the canon. The run's own Stop sweep reds on a pack edit that leaves the number alone.
37	- **Open a PR against `main`** on a per-run-unique branch — one PR for the whole run's accepted lessons (a minted stub is the exception: its own PR). Never a direct push. Keep every commit and PR terse. **Put the issue reference in the commit message** (`Refs #<n>` for the tracker below) — the `basics` `task-lifecycle` check reds CI on a promote commit that cites none.
38	
39	### 5. Log the run to the tracker
40	
41	Append a dated comment for every run that promoted at least one lesson, and for any notable rejection.
42	
43	## Tracking issue
44	
45	The standing self-improvement log is the issue titled exactly **`Claudinite tracker: Promote to Canon`**.
46	
47	- **Find it by that exact title, never a fuzzy match or a hard-coded number** (a bare number can dangle).
48	- **Create it already closed if missing** — creation always lands an issue open and ignores a `state: closed` argument, so create it and close it in a second call. **Never open, close, or reopen it** afterward — its state carries no meaning; only the log does.
49	- Log each run as a **dated comment** — not a sub-issue, so history accumulates in one scrollable feed — the date, and per lesson: the origin repo, the **ladder rung it landed on** (check id / skill / owning doc, with the named reason when prose was the fallback), and the generalized rule (or, for a notable rejection, the reason and the existing rule that already covers it).
50	
51	## What this task must never do
52	
53	- **Never mine outside a local pack** — product source, task scripts, code comments, and config are out of scope; only a local pack's `RULES.md` prose and its own check modules are candidates.
54	- **Never promote a product-specific or one-off item** — it stays in that project's local packs.
55	- **Never weaken, restate, or duplicate an existing rule** — fold a genuine sharpening in per [item-routing.md](../../item-routing.md) instead.
56	- **Never widen past the Context member list**, and **never touch a member repo** — this task only reads members and writes the canon PR.
57	- **Every step is a judgment call** (portability, duplication, ownership, how to generalize without distorting), and a plausible-but-wrong *acceptance* is what the owner's review is least likely to catch.
58

1 # gcec rules 2 3 The project's standing working rules — injected at session start while this pack 4 is declared. Activity-scoped procedures live in this pack's skills 5 (snapshot-approval, merge-and-ci, testing-guide) and surface on 6 demand; the extractor-automation domain's standing rules are the "Extractor 7 pipeline" section below, and its scheduled tasks live under `tasks/`. 8 9 ## Working rules 10 11 - **Never carry uncommitted edits onto a new branch with 12 `git checkout -- `** — that restores the paths' *committed* 13 content, silently destroying exactly the edits it was meant to preserve. 14 `git checkout -b origin/main` already brings a clean working tree along; 15 when it can't, commit or `git stash` first and never in the same `&&` chain 16 that moves the branch. In #734 the combined one-liner wiped three finished 17 edits **and** invalidated the `check_the_world.mjs` + `npm run test:offline` 18 pass that had just gone green, forcing a full re-verification. 19 - **A duplicate dispatch-trigger arriving while a session's own delegated 20 subagent is still running is a signal to stop, not to investigate.** 21 Confirm it via `resolve-dispatch` (the "not mine, change nothing" case) and 22 end the turn — don't let that check snowball into re-reading the subagent's 23 targets and redoing its work. In #876 a dispatched `tidy-issues` subagent 24 was still running in the background when a duplicate webhook fired; the 25 top-level session's "just confirming" pass over all 16 target issues 26 escalated into closing one and posting reconfirmation comments on the 27 rest — duplicating, not verifying, work its own subagent was already 28 producing — and converged the dispatch issue on that duplicate instead of 29 the subagent's actual output. 30 - **Cap and qualify every GitHub MCP list/search call** — an unbounded one 31 hard-fails the tool-result cap and costs a 2–3-call dig through the saved 32 result file. `search_issues` handed a bare title string full-text-searches the 33 whole repo and returns every match with its full body: the standing 34 `Claudinite tracker: ` lookup that opens every scheduled task blew up at 35 185–211 KB three times (#734 twice, #753), and `actions_list` without a page 36 cap at 155 KB (#760). Qualify the query (`in:title "Claudinite tracker: 37 "`, or `list_issues` + `labels`) **and** pass a small `perPage` (5–10) — 38 the answer wanted is one issue or one run, never a page of them. `perPage` 39 alone isn't the whole fix: even a single matched issue's full body can be 40 100+ KB, so the same overflow recurred with `in:title` correctly set but 41 `perPage` left off (#879, #890, #896). Pass `fields` too (e.g. `['number', 42 'title', 'state']`) to strip the body outright — a query that added it 43 (#886) returned instantly at ~3 KB where the identical unfielded query the 44 day before (#879) overflowed at 113 KB. 45 - **This repo's one divergence from the canon merge recipe: CI must be green 46 first** — twice for e2e/heavy-browser changes. The project mechanics of driving 47 a merge (dispatching CI in a web session, the poll back-off, when to arm 48 auto-merge instead of waiting) are the merge-and-ci skill — **load it for any PR a session opens**, including one 49 opened incidentally mid-task by an unattended run, not only for a deliberate 50 merge. 51 - **`npm run regen` is the regenerator** (load lists + UI snapshots + 52 generic-coverage baseline/report); a stale artifact can't slip through — its 53 own gate fails. If `regen` reports a coverage regression, that's the real gate 61 firing — review it, don't paper over it. 62 - **Keep divergence small**: when syncing a branch to `origin/main` (by rebase), 63 **run `npm run regen`** as part of the sync, so the branch carries 64 freshly-generated artifacts, not just the latest sources. 65 66 ## Owner commands 67 68 - **"bump version"** = cut a release **end to end** — bump, merge, and wait for 69 the published artifact. The bump mechanics are the canon `bump-version` 70 skill's; honor an explicit target ("bump version to 1.4.0") or level ("bump 71 patch" / "bump major") when given. Open the PR, 72 get CI green, squash-merge with `(#N)` — 73 saying "bump version" is itself the merge authorization for **this** 74 deterministic bump PR only. The merge triggers **Release: Create Package**; 75 do **not** report done until the `vX.Y.Z` GitHub Release with its refreshed 76 `google-calendar-event-creator.zip` asset is published — poll via the GitHub 77 MCP tools on the merge-and-ci skill's back-off. 78 - **"learned lessons"** = run the canon lessons-learned pass over the current 79 conversation on **the strongest model available**. Capture routing: see below. 80 81 ## Testing invariants 82 83 - **Integration cases are the reviewed contract** — a person reads 84 `dev/requirements/extractor/expected/`; nobody reviews the unit tests. Every 85 required change or bugfix gets a case (one real, focused page per distinct 86 behavior; keep cases minimal). Unit tests under `extension-test/` are a 87 supplementary safety net for page-independent logic. 88 - **`extension-test/` mirrors `extension/`'s tree, one test per source file** 89 (`extension//.js` → `extension-test//.test.js`). 90 Deliberate departures: `extension-test/integration/` for 91 whole-extension/interaction tests; no mirror for `custom/*` sources or 92 data/markup files (covered by live cases / snapshots / drift guards); 93 `extension-test/harness.js` is shared infra (not a test) and stays at the 94 root. 95 - **The pinned `REFERENCE_NOW`** (`dev/requirements/shared/reference-time.js`, 96 currently 2026-06-01) **is the floor of the cases' dates**: author a 97 neutral/upcoming case **on or after it** so it's pill-free; use a past date or 98 a future year only when the case is *pinning* a pill. 99 100 ## Codebase gotchas 101 102 Project-wide footguns only. Adding or refreshing a cached live case by hand is the 148 [testing-guide](skills/testing-guide/SKILL.md) skill. 149 150 - **All page fetching goes through [`scraperapi.mjs`](tasks/create-extractor/scraperapi.mjs), from a 151 task's preprocessing worker and nowhere else.** A rendered fetch through 152 ScraperAPI's residential proxy (`render=true`, so a single-page app records 153 post-render HTML with real data). Resolution lives in `helpers/dates.js` 180 (`parseDateFromText` / `normalizeDateValue` take a `dayFirst` flag, threaded 181 from `generic-extractor.js`'s `pageUsesDayFirstDates`), mirroring 182 `derive-timezone.js`'s locale read; unambiguous dates (a part > 12) and the 183 `.` / `-` separators are always day-first regardless (#686). 184 - **An unrecordable page is a dead end, not a failed run.** When a fetch can't 185 produce a page (bot wall, dead URL, empty render), create-extractor's 186 preprocessing labels the request `needs-human` with the reason 187 and exits **0** — a task failure would converge to a `needs-human` dispatch 188 issue as well, duplicating the signal and implying the pipeline broke when it 189 correctly declined. (`GCal.extract()` 200 alone no longer answers this: the generic extractor is the base layer of every 201 extraction now, so on a supported host its output already carries the site's 202 overrides.) Most start/end *differences* vs a dedicated source are just its 203 hardcoded `ctz` localizing to floating time (same instant), not extraction 204 bugs; the real gaps are fields it can't know generically (durations, 205 site-specific descriptions, and — where the page doesn't declare corroborating 206 hints, see `helpers/derive-timezone.js` — `ctz`). This is the comparison the 207 generic-coverage gate automates — and a case where it shows NO gap is a 208 candidate for deleting the per-site source and listing the host in 209 `supportedDomains`). 210 211 ## Architecture rules of the road 212 213 Whenever we agree on a new or changed top-level architectural guideline, update 214 this section as part of the same change (the design doc itself is 215 `dev/procedures/highLevelDesign.md`): 216 217 - **`extension/event-extractors/custom/` is the extensibility point — one file 218 per site, and nothing else.** The rest of `event-extractors/` is the pipeline 219 itself: the registry, the orchestrator, the shared helpers, and the one core 220 generic extractor (`generic-extractor.js`), which is a different kind of thing 221 from a per-site file. 222 - **The core generic extractor is the base layer of every extraction** — it runs 223 on every page, and a per-site source is only a layer of *overrides* merged over 224 it, stating the fields it gets better. A source never re-reads what the page 225 already says about itself, and the generic extractor may never know about a 226 specific site. 227 - **Being supported is DECLARED, never derived from the extractors.** 228 `supportedDomains` in `extension/host-lists.json` is the one list of hosts 229 we claim, read directly by the toolbar worker and the popup. Never add a second 230 list, and never register a placeholder source just to make a host count as 231 supported. The only guarded direction is that every per-site source's host 232 appears in the list. 233 - **A site we fully support gets no extractor file when there is nothing to 234 override.** It stays listed in `supportedDomains` and stays fully supported — 235 green icon, no correction prompt — with no file at all. When a 236 `custom/.js` shrinks to nothing, just delete it; when such a site starts 237 needing a fix the generic extractor can't make site-agnostically, add the file 238 back. Never keep a file whose only content is a restatement of the generic 239 base, and never annotate one as "nothing to add". 240 - Adding support for a new host is the most common change — the architecture 241 must keep it a single-file change: a host added to `supportedDomains`, plus — 242 only when the generic extractor gets that site wrong — one self-contained new 243 `extension/event-extractors/custom/.js` and a regenerated load list, 244 touching nothing else and assuming nothing about other extractors. 245 246 ## Capture policy — lessons land in the local packs 247 248 Route each lesson to its section here: extractor-automation to the "Extractor 249 pipeline" section, everything else to the fitting section. 250

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-branch-status: Assess one branch's landed status — merged, already-in-main, superseded, orphaned, or genuine unmerged work — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single branch is safe to delete, judging by content not the ref's name (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-branches task hands you branches to assess).
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
- writing-claudinite-skills: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus — SKILL.md conventions, where a skill's checks and tests live, catalog and pack wiring. Use when creating or editing a pack's skills/<name>/ in the canon; a consumer project's own agent docs are authoring-agent-docs' turf.
- writing-migration-plans: Where a plan and a design live, and how to order a plan's phases so nothing stalls mid-run — the plan is a tracking issue (never a plan document in the repo), the design doc carries only the end state with rationale and alternatives; front-load the out-of-band setup, write ALL the code including the cleanup and take one approval for the stack, then chain every execution step to the verification of the one before it as a queued continuation, and keep the tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan — including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file — and when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.mjs or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- canary-role: What ClaudiniteCanary is for and how to work in it — the live canary for Claudinite's consumer-safety gate. Use before changing anything in this repo, and when a canary rehearsal comes back red and you have to decide what the red means.
- git-github-advanced: Git/GitHub procedures beyond the baseline lifecycle. Use for commit layering, recovering a branch after a squash-merge, CI-trigger rules, GitHub Actions gotchas, or merge-relocation traps.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- merge-to-main: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
- site-visual-check: Screenshot and visually verify site/ (claudinite.com), desktop and mobile, and deliver the result to the owner. Use when changing site/ markup, CSS, or animations, or when checking responsive/mobile rendering.
- chrome-store-releases: The Chrome Web Store release standard every extension repo of ours ships — the vendored release workflows and composite actions, .github/release.config, versioning and the packaged artifact, the store secrets, the README install sections, and the manual Chrome Web Store steps. Use when setting up an extension repo to publish, changing or debugging its release pipeline, when asked to "bump version" on an extension repo, or when a cer/ check fires.
- bump-version: Raise the project's version — a minor bump by default. Use when the owner says "bump version".
- start-a-new-fringe-year: Set up and run the pipeline for a new Edinburgh Fringe year (a new years/<YYYY>/ folder). Use when asked to start, bootstrap, or plan a Fringe year the repo does not have data for yet — e.g. "set up 2027", "start next year".
- static-site-releases: The release standard every static-site repo of ours ships — the date-anchored version scheme, release-on-push, the explicit publish set, .github/site.config, the vendored workflows, the Pages deploy, and the setup a new site repo needs. Use when setting up a site repo, changing or debugging its release pipeline or site.config, when asked to "bump version" on a site repo, or when a static-website check fires.
- merge-and-ci: Drive this repo's PR-to-merged flow cheaply — when to open the PR, how to get CI green in a Claude web session, how to poll without wasting wall time or tokens, and when to arm auto-merge instead of waiting. Use whenever a session opens, watches, or lands a PR here — including one opened incidentally mid-task by an unattended or scheduled run, and any moment you ask "is CI green yet?" — not only for a deliberate merge or an e2e/heavy/UI change.
- snapshot-approval: Get owner approval for a moved UI-snapshot baseline. Use whenever a change to a dev/requirements case (its spec or its rendering) makes the snapshot tests fail — the pixels moved and the baseline wants to change.
- testing-guide: Map of this repo's test suites, the requirements model, and where each harness documents itself. Use before writing or changing tests here, adding a requirement case, or debugging a suite — the invariants live in the gcec pack's RULES.md; this is the deeper how-to.
- engineering-practices: General software-engineering practices — naming by scope, single-source-of-truth with drift guards, GENERATED-file discipline, earning each dependency, verifying real platform behavior. Use before writing or editing code.
- create-release-plan: The Firebase release standard — two separate dev/prod projects with the committed default pinned to dev, prod config injected only by the release pipeline, App Check attestation gating, and deliberate promotion. Use when planning a Firebase-backed app's first release, splitting a project into dev and prod, or wiring prod config and App Check into a release pipeline.
- paper-intake: Take a research paper PDF into references/ — folder, digest, extracted figures, cropped panels, calibration, synthesis. Use whenever a new article is added to this repo, or an existing one needs re-processing.
- vessel-overlay-review: Show a vessel-extraction result as an annotated overlay on the original panel and state explicit visual assertions about it. Use whenever proposing, revising, or reporting on the segmentation/measurement pipeline in this repo — before quoting any new numbers.
- map-a-data-source: Reconnaissance on a website you want data from but don't control — locate the real data surface (hydration blob, client API, or markup) and write the findings down before any parser exists. Use when adding a new source to a scraper, or when an existing source stops parsing and you suspect the site changed shape.
- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one — Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.

Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
