1	# macOS
2	
3	Portable practices for a **native macOS app** — the ones that are true whatever the app does:
4	assembling the app bundle, the TCC and Hardened Runtime pair, the Developer ID → notarization →
5	DMG lane, and the process-lifecycle facts a Mac app cannot get wrong. A default to adapt, not a
6	contract.
7	
8	Distilled from a fleet project shipping a menu-bar agent app built with SwiftPM and published as a
9	notarized DMG. Mac App Store submission is a different track — see `app-store-release`; an iPhone
10	target is `ios`.
11	
12	## The app bundle is assembled, not built
13	
14	- **SwiftPM builds a binary; nothing builds you a `.app`.** `swift build -c release` yields an
15	  executable — the bundle (`Contents/MacOS/<exe>`, `Contents/Info.plist`,
16	  `Contents/Resources/`) is assembled by your own script. Keep that script the single place the
17	  bundle's shape is defined, so the local build and CI produce byte-identical layouts.
18	- **Commit one high-resolution icon master and generate the `.icns`** in the build script (`sips`
19	  to each size into an `.iconset`, then `iconutil -c icns`). Both tools ship with macOS, so the
20	  repo carries one PNG instead of ten, and the icon can't half-update.
21	- **A menu-bar-only app is `LSUIElement: true`** in `Info.plist` — that, not code, is what removes
22	  the Dock icon and the main window.
23	- **Pin `LSMinimumSystemVersion` to the same OS version the package's `platforms:` declares.** They
24	  are two independent claims about the same floor, and only one of them is enforced at launch.
25	
26	## TCC and the Hardened Runtime are two different gates — know which applies
27	
28	Every protected resource needs a **usage-description string** in `Info.plist` (the text of the
29	consent prompt; without it the app is killed rather than prompted) — one key per resource, and they
30	are separate keys for capabilities that feel like one feature: `NSMicrophoneUsageDescription` covers
31	audio input, `NSSpeechRecognitionUsageDescription` covers the Speech framework, and an app that
32	listens *and* transcribes needs both or is killed at whichever it forgot. What each string says is
33	what the user consents to. Only *some* resources also need a **codesign entitlement**, and only
34	under the Hardened Runtime:
35	
36	- **Notarization requires the Hardened Runtime** (`codesign --options runtime`), and under it a
37	  resource-access exception must be granted explicitly by entitlement — device capture
38	  (`com.apple.security.device.audio-input`, camera) is the classic one. So **turning on
39	  notarization can silently break a capability an ad-hoc build had**, because the ad-hoc build was
40	  never running under the restriction. Ship the entitlement in the same change as the runtime flag.
41	- **Capabilities gated purely by TCC plus their usage string need no entitlement at all** (speech
42	  recognition is the worked example). Adding one you don't need is noise; omitting one you do need
43	  is a runtime failure no build step catches.
44	- **Do not enable the App Sandbox on the Developer ID track.** The sandbox belongs to the Mac App
45	  Store lane, needs a different (Apple Distribution) certificate, and silently removes
46	  capabilities the direct-download build has — distributed notifications, for one.
47	
48	## Speech recognition leaves the machine unless you say it must not
49	
50	- **`SFSpeechRecognizer` streams audio to Apple's servers by default.** On-device recognition is
51	  opt-in, and the opt-in is a property of the **request**
52	  (`request.requiresOnDeviceRecognition = true`), not of the recognizer — so it has to be set on
53	  every request the app builds, and a new call site added later starts out server-side. Nothing in
54	  the build says which mode ran; the difference is only visible in what left the machine.
55	- **The opt-in is only honourable where the locale's model is installed.** `supportsOnDeviceRecognition`
56	  is per-recognizer and false until then, and requiring on-device recognition where it isn't
57	  supported fails the request rather than quietly falling back — so check it and decide the degrade
58	  deliberately (refuse the feature, or say plainly that this locale would transcribe off-device).
59	- Speech is TCC-gated, so it needs its usage string and **no** entitlement — see the section above.
60	
61	## Keep signing and notarization an optional, secret-gated lane
62	
63	- **The unsigned path must stay a working path.** Gate the Developer ID + notarization steps on the
64	  signing secrets being present, and ship an **ad-hoc-signed** artifact when they aren't. Make
65	  signing a required step and every fork, and every build in a repo whose secrets aren't set, goes
66	  red for a reason unrelated to the change.
67	- **An ad-hoc signature cannot be notarized.** They are separate lanes, not degrees of the same
68	  one: only an identity-signed bundle can be submitted to the notary service. Don't write a
69	  pipeline that "tries" to notarize whatever it just signed.
70	- **Notarize the distributed container, then staple it** (`notarytool submit --wait`, then `stapler
71	  staple` and `stapler validate`). Stapling is what makes the download open offline without a
72	  round-trip to Apple; skipping it works on your machine and fails on a user's.
73	- **In CI, an imported identity must be in the searchable keychain list.** Creating an ephemeral
74	  keychain, importing the `.p12` and setting the key partition list is not enough —
75	  `codesign` searches the *user's keychain list*, so the new keychain has to be added to it or the
76	  identity is simply not found.
77	- **Say out loud, in a build annotation, which lane ran.** "No signing secret — publishing an
78	  ad-hoc build" turns a silently-degraded artifact into a visible one.
79	
80	## Distribution and the Gatekeeper story you owe the user
81	
82	- **A drag-to-install DMG is a staged folder, not Finder scripting.** Stage the `.app` beside a
83	  symlink to `/Applications`, drop the icon in as `.VolumeIcon.icns`, flag the folder as having a
84	  custom icon, and let `hdiutil create` carry it through. Anything that automates Finder to lay out
85	  the window is fragile in CI and unnecessary.
86	- **Write the Gatekeeper bypass for the OS your users are on.** macOS 15 removed the
87	  right-click → *Open* bypass; the current path is System Settings → Privacy & Security →
88	  *Open Anyway*, or `xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine <app>`. An install doc that still says
89	  right-click → Open reads as broken software.
90	- **A notarized build should need none of that** — if your README's manual-bypass section is the
91	  one users actually follow, the signing lane isn't running.
92	
93	## Assume the user's Mac has no developer toolchain
94	
95	The machine running a distributed app installed the artifact; it has no Xcode. Two consequences:
96	
97	- **Diagnostics belong inside the shipped app**, or in a script using only what ships with macOS.
98	  Anything requiring a compiler on the user's machine is a diagnostic that will never be run.
99	- **`command -v swift` does not test for a Swift toolchain.** `/usr/bin/swift` exists on every Mac
100	  as a stub that pops the *"install the command line developer tools?"* dialog when invoked — so
101	  the probe passes and the script asks the user to install several gigabytes of Xcode. Gate on
102	  `xcode-select -p >/dev/null 2>&1`, which fails quietly when the tools are absent.
103	
104	## Exit paths: `applicationWillTerminate` is not "every exit"
105	
106	- **`NSApplication` installs no signal handlers.** `NSApp.terminate` (menu Quit, ⌘Q, the
107	  logout/shutdown Apple Event) runs `applicationWillTerminate`; a bare `SIGTERM` (Activity
108	  Monitor's Quit, `killall`), `SIGINT` or `SIGHUP` kills the process with **no** teardown. Route
109	  them through a `DispatchSourceSignal` into `NSApp.terminate` — and set `signal(sig, SIG_IGN)`
110	  **before** `resume()`, or a signal arriving in the gap still takes the fatal default.
111	  `SIGKILL`, Force Quit and a crash stay uncoverable; name that as residual risk rather than
112	  claiming coverage.
113	- **An uncaught Objective-C exception is an exit path too.** It aborts the process, so no teardown
114	  runs; a framework call that *raises* (rather than throws) is therefore a resource-release bug as
115	  well as a crash. Swift cannot catch `NSException` — a tiny Objective-C target of your own is the
116	  only trap, and it is only safe around calls that validate before mutating.
117	
118	## Sleep, wake, and deferred work
119	
120	- **There is no "the machine is back" notification.** `NSWorkspace.didWakeNotification` also fires
121	  for a dark/Power-Nap wake with nobody there. Fan in the several signals that a real return emits
122	  (wake, screens wake, session became active, the screen-unlocked distributed notification) and
123	  **coalesce them** — a genuine return fires a burst, and each must not schedule its own work.
124	- **Coalesce with an id, not a boolean.** A single `pending` flag deadlocks: something invalidates
125	  the timer, the timer clears the flag, and whichever ordering loses leaves the next wake either
126	  unable to schedule or double-scheduling. Hold the in-flight work's id; a stale timer compares its
127	  captured id and returns.
128	- **`asyncAfter` work scheduled before sleep fires immediately on wake.** Give every intentional
129	  stop a generation counter, capture the generation when scheduling, and abort in the closure if it
130	  moved — otherwise deferred work reacquires resources on the way *into* sleep or before the
131	  machine has settled. When cancelling in-flight work, reset the latches beside it too, or they
132	  stay stuck and block everything after.
133	- **Measure a span that includes a sleep with `Date()`, not `ProcessInfo.systemUptime`.** The
134	  monotonic clock does not advance while the machine sleeps — which is exactly the span you are
135	  trying to measure. Use `systemUptime` for the opposite question ("how long, while we were
136	  awake").
137	
138	## Holding a device the user can unplug
139	
140	If the app captures from shared hardware (microphone, camera), these are the rules that cost the
141	most to learn:
142	
143	- **Release the device on every path where capture ends.** A process that dies with its IO proc
144	  still registered can leave some USB devices wedged until physically re-plugged. This is necessary
145	  and *not sufficient* — a device can also wedge below the user-space audio daemon, where no
146	  teardown of yours helps.
147	- **Never construct a capture engine to ask whether a device exists.** Materializing an input node
148	  opens the default device and mints a hidden per-client aggregate device; a retry ladder built on
149	  that is not a cheap probe but an open/close plus an aggregate create-and-destroy, repeated for as
150	  long as the hardware is missing. Query the HAL's device properties instead — a property read
151	  opens nothing and can be sampled forever for free. The churn is observable rather than
152	  theoretical: each hidden aggregate appears in the HAL as `CADefaultDeviceAggregate-<pid>-<n>`, so
153	  what a retry ladder is really doing can be counted instead of argued about.
154	- **Presence is not usability, at either layer.** Mid-teardown a device enumerates as alive with an
155	  unreadable name and a **zero** sample rate. Require a nonzero rate and a sane channel count, and
156	  judge the *system default* input — a healthy device behind a broken default is not one you can
157	  capture from. One layer up, the engine lies in the opposite direction: with the input torn down,
158	  the input node's `outputFormat(forBus: 0)` still reports a plausible 48 kHz while its
159	  `inputFormat` reports 0, so a guard written against the wrong one waves through starts that
160	  cannot succeed — read both and require them to agree. Whatever a new probe reads, ask what that
161	  field says while the device is absent.
162	- **A duration is a claim about a span you observed.** "It has been present for N seconds" is only
163	  as good as the observation behind it: a state maintained by a timer must be **seeded at start**
164	  (a repeating timer does not fire immediately) and **invalidated across any gap** — a sleep is a
165	  gap, and carrying a settle clock straight through one makes the gate inert on exactly the
166	  transition it was built for. Model "not observed" as its own state, distinct from "absent", and
167	  key the span on the device's **UID** — an unplug-and-replug, or a swap for a different mic, is a
168	  new arrival that starts its own clock rather than inheriting the departed device's.
169	- **"Started" is not "working".** A running engine delivering buffers of pure silence looks
170	  identical to a healthy one from the inside. Measure what actually arrives, publish a health state
171	  the UI renders, and when a failure mode has exactly one remedy, name **that** remedy rather than
172	  the generic one.
173	- **Compile-green is not a gate for device code.** `swift build` cannot see a raise-vs-throw bug or
174	  a lifecycle race, and both are reachable in the first second of a run. A change here is not
175	  verified until the app has actually launched on a Mac. Reaching the interesting case needs no
176	  hardware theatre: let the display sleep and `coreaudiod` tears its device contexts down seconds
177	  later, which is the same transition as an unplug from the app's point of view.
178

1	# Evaluating and routing a new item
2	
3	The shared method for three decisions every proposed addition to this corpus must pass through: **is it worthy** of inclusion at all, **which mechanism** should carry it, and — only for prose — **where does it go**. Any routine or person that adds an item — the [growth promote stage](tasks/growth-promote/task.md), an owner-requested retrospective pass, a hand edit — applies this same protocol, so the decision-making lives here once instead of being re-derived per caller.
4	
5	This is a Claudinite-internal doc used by the growth lifecycle (see [the canon-curation README](README.md)): it is **not** part of the mounted corpus and consuming repos do not `@import` it.
6	
7	An "item" is one **distilled, portable rule** — not a transcript, not a narration of what happened. A candidate still phrased as "here's what we did" has not been distilled yet and is below the bar on form alone, before any of the tests below. This doc picks up once a distilled rule exists and decides its fate.
8	
9	## Worthiness — does it earn a place at all
10	
11	The corpus is read read-only by every consuming repo, so a **duplicative** item (already covered) or an **undistilled** one (a story or a truism, not a rule) pollutes shared canon and costs every future reader. The bar guards against *those* — it is **not** a bar on *scope*: an item useful to only one project today can still earn a place (see Portable). Admit an item only when **all** hold:
12	
13	- **Distilled.** It is a single tight rule in the imperative, not a story, a log, or a restatement of a generic truism.
14	- **Portable — would a *future* project benefit?** Not "useful to every project today." An item can help only **one** project right now and still belong here, so long as another project — **especially one with a similar tech stack or process** — would benefit when it arrives. Being specific to a technology or a process is **not** disqualifying: generalize it and route it to that technology's or practice's home. What disqualifies is leaning on *this* project's non-transferable particulars — a product requirement, or a one-off incident in how it happened to call some API. The test, a genuinely hard one: *if another project with a similar tech stack came along, would it benefit from this?* Yes → portable; only-ever-this-product → local. A rule mined from Claudinite's own test suite is the hardest case: it reads as generic testing craft even when it actually depends on Claudinite's own shape — the only project whose tests build git-repo fixtures because its checks take a repo as input. Before promoting one, grep the fleet's own callers of the pattern the rule is about; zero callers outside this project's own conformance tests means the lesson is local however general its wording (#857: a fixture-signing rule read as portable, was promoted to `writing-tests`, then reverted once every caller of the fixture helper turned out to be a Claudinite conformance test).
15	- **Durable and reusable.** It will still apply on a future, unseen task — not a one-off, not a situational detail, not something already implied by an existing rule.
16	- **Readable through the channel it lands in.** A rule whose premise is that the delivery channel
17	  itself failed cannot be carried by that channel. Promote #497 admitted "the tell that the SessionStart
18	  hook did not fire" as pack prose — and pack prose is what that hook delivers, so in the one situation
19	  the rule describes it is not in context to be read. Detecting a channel's own failure belongs in code,
20	  not in the payload the channel carries; reject such an item here rather than rewording it.
21	- **Not already covered.** The insight does not already exist **anywhere** in the corpus, even worded differently or owned by a different file. This is checked against the *entire* corpus, not just the file it would land in — see [Dedupe against the whole corpus](#dedupe-against-the-whole-corpus).
22	
23	Reject on any miss — but the misses that matter are *undistilled*, *already-covered*, or *genuinely one-off*, not merely *narrow*. When you're torn over a real, non-duplicate rule, lean toward **keeping** it — the goal is a broad library. When you're torn over whether something is a duplicate, or a rule at all, leave it out. The failure to avoid is padding the canon with restatements of what's already there; admitting a narrow-but-reusable rule is not that failure.
24	
25	### Dedupe against the whole corpus
26	
27	Before admitting anything, read across the corpus, not only the file you expect to own the item. The same insight is frequently already present under a different heading or in an adjacent group. If it sharpens an **existing** rule, fold it in with a minimal edit rather than adding a second bullet that says nearly the same thing — and never weaken or restate what is already there in the process.
28	
29	**Sweep last, and case-insensitively.** A dedupe pass is only evidence about the text it actually read, so it runs **after** every re-home, merge and edit the change makes — a sweep run early and never re-run reports clean on content that has since moved under it. Measured on #740 (the seven-PR promote consolidation): the sweep ran *before* two lessons were re-homed out of a folded-away skill file into `packs/basics/RULES.md`, and **three** copies of the same unknown-state rule reached the owner, who found them by reading. The re-run then surfaced a further pair the pattern had missed because it was case-sensitive and the survivors were capitalised. So: sweep as the last step, match case-insensitively, and state the similarity threshold you swept at so the "no remaining near-duplicates" claim is checkable.
30	
31	## Mechanism triage — prose is the fallback, not the default
32	
33	A worthy item next descends the **promotion ladder** ([../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md) owns it): platform setting (always paired with its verifying check) → PreToolUse hook → conformance check → skill → prose. The *first* rung that can carry the item wins — a rule about repo state becomes a check whose failure message *is* the lesson; a bad action to prevent becomes a guard; a procedure or knowledge with a nameable trigger becomes (or joins) a skill. Only an item none of those can carry — judgment, in-flight behavior, signature-less knowledge — proceeds to the file routing below, and its landing **names that reason** in the promote log so conversion rates stay auditable.
34	
35	**"No universal signature" alone never routes an item to prose.** A rule converts to a check when a *narrow, file-scoped* signature covers the **grounded cases** — the concrete shapes the rule was distilled from — even though no signature covers every conceivable violation. Gate it relevance-first so it stays inert off-target, and document the genuinely signature-less residue in the rule's own comments as out of scope. The prose rung is only for an item whose grounded cases *themselves* have no reliable signature (pure judgment, runtime/in-flight behavior).
36	
37	## Routing — picking the right file (rung-5 items only)
38	
39	Routing is robust when it keys on **stable file groups**, not on the current roster of individual files (which grows over time). The corpus is organized into a few groups, each with its own selection rule:
40	
41	1. **The practice group** — durable, project-agnostic practices, each file a self-contained, reusable unit of know-how the agent applies whenever its subject comes up (engineering, agentic, git/GitHub, testing, investigation, discipline, architecture), partitioned **by kind of practice** with each file owning one recurring subject cluster. This group spans **two folders that differ only by *when* the rule loads**: `always/` for a rule that applies to essentially every task (the index `@`-imports it, so it's force-loaded every session), and `tasks/` for a subject-gated rule read on demand when its trigger fires. Route in two steps: first match the item's *kind* to the file whose cluster already owns that subject; then keep it in `always/` only if it genuinely isn't tied to one kind of task (the rare case — `always/` stays small), otherwise it belongs in `tasks/`. Read the group's own index (the root `CLAUDE.md`) to find the current owner for a kind — never from memory, since the set of clusters can grow.
42	2. **The per-user group** — interaction preferences and trigger phrases. This group does **not live in this repo**: an item of this kind routes out to the person it belongs to, never into the practice group and never back into the canon.
43	3. **The per-technology group** — practices specific to one technology, **one file per technology**. Route a technology-specific item to that technology's file. When **no pack homes that technology** (not even a stub), the item doesn't land in a loose doc — it **mints a fingerprinted stub pack** (a `packs/<tech>/`, delivered in its own PR), so the next project on that stack self-declares it; [promote](tasks/growth-promote/task.md)'s stub-minting floor and [the generate-project-instructions skill](../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/skills/generate-project-instructions/SKILL.md) own the mechanics.
44	
45	Pick **exactly one** owner. If an item plausibly fits two files, choose the single best one — never split one item across files, and never duplicate it into both. The group decides the *axis* (kind, person, or technology); the file within the group is then the one whose existing scope the item falls squarely inside.
46	
47	### When nothing fits
48	
49	An item that matches **no** existing file is **not** a reject signal by itself — a genuinely new category of lesson is meant to be learnable, so a worthy item that no file owns earns its own file. Resolve it in this order:
50	
51	- **Route into an existing owner** when one genuinely fits — the first choice. If the item belongs to a file's cluster and merely sits slightly off-center, a small stretch toward that owner beats spinning up a new file. A new file is for when no existing file's scope genuinely fits, **not** a way to dodge folding into an existing owner.
52	- **Open a new file** when the item clears the [Worthiness](#worthiness--does-it-earn-a-place-at-all) bar in full — distilled, portable, durable and reusable, and not already covered anywhere in the corpus — **and** no existing file's scope genuinely fits it. That is the whole bar: nothing more is required. Do **not** also demand that you expect the cluster to recur, that forcing the item into the closest file would *distort* it, or default to rejecting when the new-file call is a close one — those extra hurdles are dropped. Creating a file obliges registering it where the corpus is indexed and in any routing table, in the **same** change, so it never lands orphaned (see [Keep the write surface bounded](#keep-the-write-surface-bounded)).
53	
54	The loosening above is **only** to the new-cluster hurdle, never to the per-item bar. An item that misses [Worthiness](#worthiness--does-it-earn-a-place-at-all) — a one-off, non-portable or project-specific, a restatement of a generic truism, or already covered anywhere in the corpus — is rejected whether or not a file already exists for it; for the per-item admission decision, the default-to-reject-when-unsure tiebreak still stands.
55	
56	## Keep the write surface bounded
57	
58	Once worthiness and routing are settled, the edit touches **only** the single owning file: add or sharpen one terse rule in that file's existing voice and format, and change nothing else. Do not "improve" unrelated rules while you are in there. The sole exception is the new-file path above, whose surface is itself bounded to the new file plus its index and routing-table registration.
59

1	# Growth — promote lessons into the canon (the central stage)
2	
3	The [growth lifecycle](../../README.md)'s central stage: read the target members' local packs, lift the portable lessons into the shared canon, and open a PR against the canon's default branch **for the owner to approve**. Declared only by the Claudinite home repo, so it runs **once, centrally**, never per project.
4	
5	The run's **Context section is binding scope**: it names the exact target members (those whose local packs changed in the window). Work exactly that list — the fleet enumeration already happened in the precondition; **do not enumerate the fleet yourself or widen past the Context**.
6	
7	Promotion is the **judgment gate before shared canon**. This run opens a PR and **never arms auto-merge** — the owner approves it. But don't lean on that review as the portability check: [extract](../../../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/tasks/growth-extract/task.md) stays project-specific by design, so it's no second opinion, and the owner can't re-derive every portability call. This task's judgment is the real thing between a bad rule and every project that reads the canon — keep the bar high (dedupe against the whole corpus; default to reject when unsure).
8	
9	## Conventions used in this doc
10	
11	- **GitHub access is MCP-only** (`mcp__github__*`). You are outside each member repo — read its files over the API (get-file-contents, never a cross-repo checkout; the sandbox has no cross-repo git). The canon PR is opened over MCP too.
12	- **A member's local packs** are everything under `.claudinite/local/packs/` (the legacy `.claudinite/local_packs/` accepted during the rename window) — its own packs, never the read-only mounted canon elsewhere under `.claudinite/`.
13	- **`main`** stands for the canon's default branch.
14	
15	## What each run does
16	
17	### 1. Read the target members' local **packs**
18	
19	For each member named in Context, read its **local packs**. The candidate pool is a local pack's captured knowledge — its `RULES.md` **prose** AND its own **checks** (a `<pack>/*.mjs` rule module — its id, description, and failure message *are* a captured, enforceable lesson; the strongest promotion lifts it to a **canon check**, generalized, reusing the [prose-to-checks](../../../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/skills/prose-to-checks/SKILL.md) mechanics — or to canon prose when it doesn't generalize to a check). **Out of scope, staying put:** a lesson deliberately placed as a **code comment at its call site**, a project's task scripts, product source, and config. Never promote from product source. A genuinely portable rule that looks trapped in a code comment was mis-placed at extract time — leave it for a future extract pass to re-home into a pack. You don't need to tell new from old — the dedup step drops anything the canon already carries. No barrier holds tonight's extracts: read whatever is already **merged** on each member's default branch; anything landing mid-run is tomorrow's input.
20	
21	### 2. Generalize each candidate — *before* judging whether it belongs
22	
23	Generalize first, then decide worthiness — never the reverse. The act of generalizing is itself the portability probe — a rule that goes vacuous when lifted, or only makes sense with its project's context, isn't portable; leave it local. Work the rule standalone (origin naming and grouping carry no weight); strip the project (names, files, example stay in the origin repo — promote the distilled rule only); a **technology** mention isn't a disqualifier (lift it to the broadest scope that stays true — tech-specific is fine, *product*-specific is not); decide tool-vs-process and frame it for that home.
24	
25	### 3. Then judge worthiness — deduped against the *entire* corpus
26	
27	Holding the generalized rule, decide if it earns a place by the bar [item-routing.md](../../item-routing.md) owns (don't restate its gates). Lean **inclusive** — keep anything a future project could use — but be strict about **duplication**: dedupe against **every** corpus doc, not only the one you'd expect to own it.
28	
29	### 4. Triage the mechanism, then route
30	
31	- **Descend the promotion ladder first** ([item-routing.md](../../item-routing.md)'s mechanism triage). Prose is the fallback, not the default: a lesson a check can carry is **authored as the check** in this PR — the rule module in the right pack, the failure message carrying the generalized lesson, **plus a fixture test proving it fires** on a violating input and stays quiet on a clean one. When a confident detection-plus-fixture can't be authored unattended, land the lesson as prose **and** open a tagged conformance-backlog issue — never a silently-shipped broken check.
32	- **Route** each prose rule to its **one** owning doc ([item-routing.md](../../item-routing.md) owns the placement); match its voice and format; pick exactly one owner, never split or duplicate.
33	- **A technology with no home → mint a fingerprinted stub pack, in its own PR**, reusing the pack-writing mechanics [the generate-project-instructions skill](../../../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/skills/generate-project-instructions/SKILL.md) owns — `packs/<tech>/` with `pack.mjs` (add the `marker`/`detect` fingerprint when the technology carries a reliable one, else `detect: null`), a `RULES.md` seeded from the lesson, a `README.md`, and its `packs/README.md` index row. A minted pack ships in its **own** PR, split from the run's lesson-promotion PR (a new pack earns its own review surface). Never mint from imagination and never park an empty one to fill later — a pack minted here is populated from the *real, portable lesson* that justified it. Do not pad it with speculative rules no project earned — the "written from imagination, not distilled from worked examples" failure; an ungroundable rule isn't written. (Authoring a *fuller* pack from a technology's usage across the whole fleet — rather than a single lesson — is the per-repo pack-discovery task's job, not this floor's.) The follow-ups a fresh stub invites — enriching it from known best practices, triaging which skills it should require, spinning up dependent/aspect packs — are **not** automated here: note them for the owner and leave them to a later, deliberate pass.
34	- **Write it terse — when + what.** State the relevance (*when* it applies) and the rule (*what* to do); add a *why* only to flag severity, in a few words.
35	- **Bounded write surface — `packs/`/`skills/` only** (CI-enforced on the PR). Edit only the one owning doc — or, for a check-conversion, only the new rule module, its registration in the pack registry, and its fixture test. Don't "improve" unrelated rules while you're in there. The two bounded exceptions (both within `packs/`): the new-doc path [item-routing.md](../../item-routing.md) owns, and minting a stub pack.
36	- **Bump the `version` of every pack you edited** (`packs/<id>/pack.mjs`) — a pack's directory reaches a member only when that number exceeds the one the member has installed, so a promoted lesson left at the old version stays in the canon. The run's own Stop sweep reds on a pack edit that leaves the number alone.
37	- **Open a PR against `main`** on a per-run-unique branch — one PR for the whole run's accepted lessons (a minted stub is the exception: its own PR). Never a direct push. Keep every commit and PR terse. **Put the issue reference in the commit message** (`Refs #<n>` for the tracker below) — the `basics` `task-lifecycle` check reds CI on a promote commit that cites none.
38	
39	### 5. Log the run to the tracker
40	
41	Append a dated comment for every run that promoted at least one lesson, and for any notable rejection.
42	
43	## Tracking issue
44	
45	The standing self-improvement log is the issue titled exactly **`Claudinite tracker: Promote to Canon`**.
46	
47	- **Find it by that exact title, never a fuzzy match or a hard-coded number** (a bare number can dangle).
48	- **Create it already closed if missing** — creation always lands an issue open and ignores a `state: closed` argument, so create it and close it in a second call. **Never open, close, or reopen it** afterward — its state carries no meaning; only the log does.
49	- Log each run as a **dated comment** — not a sub-issue, so history accumulates in one scrollable feed — the date, and per lesson: the origin repo, the **ladder rung it landed on** (check id / skill / owning doc, with the named reason when prose was the fallback), and the generalized rule (or, for a notable rejection, the reason and the existing rule that already covers it).
50	
51	## What this task must never do
52	
53	- **Never mine outside a local pack** — product source, task scripts, code comments, and config are out of scope; only a local pack's `RULES.md` prose and its own check modules are candidates.
54	- **Never promote a product-specific or one-off item** — it stays in that project's local packs.
55	- **Never weaken, restate, or duplicate an existing rule** — fold a genuine sharpening in per [item-routing.md](../../item-routing.md) instead.
56	- **Never widen past the Context member list**, and **never touch a member repo** — this task only reads members and writes the canon PR.
57	- **Every step is a judgment call** (portability, duplication, ownership, how to generalize without distorting), and a plausible-but-wrong *acceptance* is what the owner's review is least likely to catch.
58

1	# macOS audio lifecycle — releasing the mic on every path
2	
3	Hard-won rules for `mac/Sources/LaughCounter/` (AudioHub, AppDelegate's restart
4	machinery, VoiceCommand). Read before touching engine start/stop, sleep/wake, or
5	exit handling.
6	
7	**The invariant.** If this process ends — or intentionally stops capture — while
8	the `AVAudioEngine` input tap's CoreAudio IOProc is still registered on the
9	device, some USB webcam mics wedge: dead/silent, no input registered in System
10	Settings, until physically re-plugged. So the tap + engine must be torn down on
11	*every* path where capture ends, and the engine must never rapid-cycle or
12	overlap restarts. (#22)
13	
14	## Never reuse an `AVAudioEngine` across a device change (#61)
15	
16	An `AVAudioEngine` caches the input hardware format when its input node is first
17	materialized, and **the cache does not follow the device**. After CoreAudio tears
18	the input down — a USB mic re-enumerating, or coreaudiod dropping its contexts
19	when the display sleeps — `inputNode.outputFormat(forBus: 0)` still reports the
20	*old* rate, while `installTap` validates against the freshly-queried hardware
21	format. They disagree, and `installTap` raises an **uncatchable** NSException:
22	`required condition is false: format.sampleRate == inputHWFormat.sampleRate`.
23	
24	This killed the app on **every** configuration change — six for six over fifteen
25	days on the owner's Mac mini, the longest outage fifteen days of nobody noticing.
26	The pre-tap guard added in #22 did not help, because it compared the stale cache
27	against itself and always passed: not the microsecond race its comment assumed,
28	but a design gap. So `AudioHub.prepareFormat()` **builds a new engine every time**
29	(stopping the old one first — dropping the last reference to a *running* engine
30	abandons its IOProc on the device, the wedge condition). Three consequences:
31	
32	- **The crash was also the mic-wedge cause.** An uncaught NSException aborts the
33	  process, so `applicationWillTerminate` never runs and the tap's IOProc is left
34	  registered — the BRIO went dead until physically re-plugged. The exit-path rule
35	  below calls crash teardown "residual risk"; at six crashes in fifteen days it
36	  was the main risk.
37	- **A replaced engine invalidates an observer bound to the old instance**, so
38	  `AudioHub` owns the `.AVAudioEngineConfigurationChange` observation and
39	  republishes it via `onConfigurationChange` (delivered on main). Registering it
40	  from `AppDelegate` against `audio.engine` would go quiet after the first
41	  restart — and a quiet config-change observer means the app stops noticing that
42	  its microphone vanished.
43	- **Swift cannot catch `NSException`**, so the last line of defence is a few
44	  lines of Objective-C (`Sources/ObjCExceptionTrap`, its own SwiftPM target — our
45	  source, not a dependency). Catching one is only safe because these calls
46	  validate *before* mutating anything; don't wrap framework calls in general.
47	  Treat the trap as **unproven** until something demonstrates it catching a real
48	  raise: the exception has to unwind through the intervening Swift closure frame,
49	  which is not guaranteed to work.
50	
51	**A new engine must have a node attached before `prepare()`.** `AVAudioEngine`
52	initializes its graph inside `prepare()` and asserts `inputNode != nullptr ||
53	outputNode != nullptr` — another uncatchable NSException. A freshly constructed
54	engine has neither: `inputNode` is created lazily *on first access*, and touching
55	the property is what attaches it. `AudioHub.makeEngine()` does that as part of
56	building one, so no call ordering elsewhere can get it wrong. The single-engine
57	code satisfied this by accident — `requestListening()`'s `stop()` reached
58	`engine.inputNode.removeTap(onBus: 0)` long before any `prepare()` — and
59	rebuilding the engine *after* that call removed the accident: v0.3.0 crashed one
60	second into every launch. (#72)
61	
62	**`outputFormat(forBus:)` cannot tell you the microphone is gone.** For the input
63	node, `inputFormat(forBus: 0)` is the *hardware* format — the one `installTap`
64	asserts on. `outputFormat(forBus: 0)` is the bus's output format, and with the
65	device torn down it still reports a plausible 48 kHz while `inputFormat` reports
66	0. Guards written against `outputFormat` therefore pass while the mic is absent
67	and leave `installTap` to raise: measured, once a minute for the whole 28 minutes
68	the displays slept. Validate `inputFormat`, and require it to agree with
69	`outputFormat`, before installing a tap. (#76)
70	
71	**The mic is unavailable for as long as the displays sleep** — on this Mac mini
72	with a Logitech BRIO, `pmset displaysleepnow` tears the input down within
73	~20 seconds and it does not return until the displays wake (28 minutes in one
74	measurement). Recovery arrives as an `.AVAudioEngineConfigurationChange` when the
75	device reappears. So a *bounded* retry ladder is the wrong shape — it expires
76	with the cause fully present — and the give-up message must not blame the
77	hardware. Back off to a ceiling and keep checking; a cheap format read once a
78	minute is nowhere near the rate that cycles a mic.
79	
80	**Compile-green is not a gate for this file.** Two crash-on-launch builds shipped
81	past CI, which only runs `swift build`. Every raise-vs-throw bug here is invisible
82	to the compiler and reachable in the first second of a run, so a change to
83	`AudioHub` is not verified until it has actually started on a Mac.
84	
85	Reproduce it without waiting for hardware to misbehave: let the display sleep
86	(`displaysleep 20`), and coreaudiod tears its contexts down seconds later.
87	
88	## `listening` never meant audio was arriving — measure the buffers (#79)
89	
90	`listening` is set because `engine.start()` returned. It has never meant a single
91	buffer arrived, and the settle-time reconciliation checks `audio.isRunning`, which
92	a running-but-dead engine also satisfies. So the app could hold a wedged device
93	for an entire evening with the menu bar reporting "listening" — the one symptom
94	the owner sees, saying the one thing that isn't true. Every round of this bug was
95	therefore reconstructed after the fact from a log whose only claim was `listening
96	started`.
97	
98	`AudioDiagnostics` closes that: the tap reports every buffer, and 15s of silence
99	while we believe we are capturing is an `AUDIO STALL` line plus a distinct menu
100	state. Three things about it are load-bearing:
101	
102	- **Read the HAL, don't build an engine, when you only want to know whether a mic
103	  is there.** `AudioObjectGetPropertyData` is a property query that does *not*
104	  open the device, so sampling it every five seconds forever is free and cannot
105	  cycle anything. `AudioHub.prepareFormat()` is the opposite — it builds an
106	  engine, materializes `inputNode` (which opens the device) and calls `prepare()`
107	  *before* validating — so the "cheap format read" the retry-ladder comment in
108	  `AppDelegate` claims is actually a full device open/close, once a minute for as
109	  long as the mic is missing.
110	- **`kAudioDevicePropertyDeviceIsRunningSomewhere` is the wedge oracle.** It is
111	  true when *any* process has IO running on the device. No buffers arriving while
112	  it is true means the running stream is ours and it is dead — as opposed to the
113	  device having gone away, which looks identical from inside the app.
114	- **Measure buffer silence with `systemUptime`, not `Date()`** — the exact
115	  opposite of the sleep-duration rule above, for the opposite reason: this is
116	  "how long has the stream been silent *while we were awake*", so a sleep in the
117	  middle must not be counted as silence.
118	
119	Log on state change, not on a timer: a heartbeat every ten minutes, and an
120	immediate line when a stall starts or ends or the device set changes. (Same
121	reason `scheduleStartRetry` announces its slow mode once — a line a minute for
122	half an hour buries everything else.)
123	
124	## Opening the default input creates an aggregate device — so a restart churns two
125	
126	The first field output from `AudioDiagnostics` showed the input device set is not
127	just the microphone:
128	
129	```
130	inputs=[*"Logitech BRIO"/usb/48000Hz/2ch/alive=y/running=n
131	        "CADefaultDeviceAggregate-70999-0"/grup/48000Hz/2ch/alive=y/running=n]
132	```
133	
134	That second entry is a **private aggregate device** (`grup` =
135	`kAudioDeviceTransportTypeAggregate`) that coreaudiod creates *per client* when
136	an app captures from the default input, so the client can survive the default
137	changing under it. It was already present in the first sample, before capture
138	started — i.e. **merely constructing `AudioHub` creates it**, because
139	`makeEngine()` materializes `inputNode`, and touching that property opens the
140	default input device.
141	
142	The consequence is that the retry ladder's cost was under-estimated twice over.
143	`prepareFormat()` → `renewEngine()` does not merely open and close the
144	microphone; it tears down and recreates an aggregate device inside coreaudiod on
145	every attempt — a much heavier operation than a device open, and one that has to
146	re-resolve the default input each time. That is what runs once a minute, for as
147	long as the mic is missing.
148	
149	It also means the *device set itself* changes on every one of those cycles, as
150	the aggregate comes and goes. So a diagnostic that alarms on "the device list
151	changed" alarms on our own restarts. Separate the two: an appearing/vanishing
152	device (or a changed rate, channel count or alive flag) is a hardware event;
153	`isRunningSomewhere` flipping is usually just us. `AudioDiagnostics.identities()`
154	is that split.
155	
156	## What the first day of field data settled — and what it did **not** (#79)
157	
158	Written down because the sections above read as a case against the retry ladder,
159	and a future session could mistake that case for a verdict. It is not one.
160	
161	**Confirmed by measurement:**
162	
163	- *The instrument is sound.* Buffer accounting is exact — 8192.0 frames per
164	  buffer against `installTap`'s `bufferSize`, 5.859 buffers/sec against a
165	  theoretical 5.859 — and it reconciles against events it shares no code with: a
166	  605s heartbeat window was missing 14.2s of audio, and the log independently
167	  recorded a 14s outage inside it.
168	- *The aggregate really is destroyed and rebuilt per restart.* The suffix in
169	  `CADefaultDeviceAggregate-<pid>-<n>` is a per-client counter; it went `-0` →
170	  `-2` across a single unplug/replug. **Use that suffix to count churn** — it is
171	  the cheapest available measure of how many times coreaudiod has rebuilt the
172	  aggregate for us.
173	- *The ladder does run at its ceiling in the wild.* One outage produced five
174	  failed starts at 63, 63, 63 and 56 seconds apart — the once-a-minute
175	  open/close cycle, observed rather than argued.
176	- *The mic leaves on its own, often.* Two spontaneous drop-outs in ~70 minutes
177	  with nobody touching the hardware. Restart cycles are frequent even when
178	  nothing sleeps, so any per-restart cost is paid far more often than a
179	  sleep/wake-shaped mental model suggests.
180	
181	**Not confirmed, and it is the whole question:** every observed episode
182	recovered cleanly — the four-minute one, the nine-second one, and the deliberate
183	replug. Churn *happens*; it has **not** been shown to cause the wedge. The wedge
184	state (menu claiming "listening", mic dead system-wide, process alive) has not
185	recurred since the diagnostics shipped. Don't write the fix until an `AUDIO
186	STALL` line with `running=y` says which theory is right.
187	
188	> **Superseded — read the next section.** The wedge did recur, and the evidence
189	> arrived in a shape this paragraph did not anticipate: there was no `AUDIO
190	> STALL` line at all. Don't wait for one.
191	
192	**A design constraint the data did settle**, for whatever cheap availability
193	probe eventually replaces the build-an-engine-to-ask approach: a device can be
194	present in the HAL, `alive=y`, and still useless. Mid-teardown the input listed
195	as `"(unnamed)"/????/0Hz/2ch/alive=y` — readable enough to enumerate, with an
196	unreadable name, unknown transport and a **zero sample rate**. So the probe must
197	require a nonzero rate (and sane channel count), not mere presence, or it will
198	wave through starts that cannot succeed — the same trap as `outputFormat` above,
199	one layer down.
200	
201	## The wedge recurred, and it lives *below* coreaudiod (#88)
202	
203	It came back on 0.4.1, and in a third shape — **no `AUDIO STALL`, ever**. Buffers
204	were arriving at the full rate (3545 per 600s against a theoretical 3515) from a
205	device reporting `alive=y/running=y/48000Hz/2ch`, and **every sample was exactly
206	zero**, for half an hour, system-wide — System Settings → Sound → Input showed a
207	dead meter too. Not the stall (buffers stopped), not the vanish (`inputs=NONE`):
208	the mode `AudioDiagnostics` had anticipated in a comment and never seen — a
209	device that is enumerated and streaming and *not capturing*.
210	
211	**The escalation ladder, tried in order, is the finding:**
212	
213	| Attempted | Cleared it |
214	| --- | --- |
215	| Quitting LaughCounter (full `applicationWillTerminate` teardown) | no |
216	| `sudo killall coreaudiod` | no |
217	| Physically unplugging and re-plugging the mic | **yes** |
218	
219	That settles what the release-the-mic invariant never could: **this wedge is not
220	in our process, and not in coreaudiod's user-space state either.** It survives
221	every client dying *and* the audio daemon being restarted from scratch; only a USB
222	re-enumeration takes the device out of it. Two consequences outrank the rest of
223	this file:
224	
225	- **No in-process recovery can work, so do not build one.** A restart ladder
226	  against this state is pure churn — it cannot succeed, and cycling is the thing
227	  we already believe is dangerous. The app's whole job here is to *notice fast,
228	  say so honestly, and name the one remedy that works.*
229	- **"Release the mic on every path" is necessary but not sufficient.** The
230	  teardown ran correctly on Quit and the device stayed wedged. A clean exit
231	  prevents the IOProc-abandonment cause; it does not prevent this one.
232	
233	**What shipped is reporting, not recovery.** `no signal` was already detected and
234	logged at ERROR every ten minutes — and it drove **nothing**: `isStalled` tripped
235	only on *absent* buffers, so the menu bar showed 😄 "listening" for the whole
236	outage while the log said the opposite. That is exactly the sin #79 set out to
237	kill, recurring one layer up, and it is why this round *again* had to be
238	reconstructed from a log instead of noticed. So `AudioDiagnostics` publishes a
239	three-state `health` (`ok` / `stalled` / `noSignal`), every user-facing surface
240	renders it, and the no-signal text says **unplug it** rather than "try Restart
241	listening" — because restarting is measured not to work. When a state has exactly
242	one remedy, the UI must name that remedy, not the generic one.
243	
244	**Detection moved off the heartbeat.** The old check ran inside the 600s heartbeat
245	block, so a dead stream was invisible for up to ten minutes and then repeated an
246	identical ERROR every ten minutes for as long as it lasted. It is judged on the 5s
247	sample tick over a 60s window of all-zero buffers now, and logged once per
248	transition. 60s is safe against a quiet room by a wide margin — a real capsule
249	always has a noise floor, and the window covers ~350 buffers.
250	
251	**"Only a replug clears it" is not "we didn't cause it."** Those are separate
252	claims and this file conflated them for one round: the ladder above establishes
253	that the state is *irreversible once triggered*, and says nothing about what
254	triggers it. The trigger question is answered below.
255	
256	## Never build an `AVAudioEngine` to ask whether a microphone exists (#88)
257	
258	This is the thing that made LaughCounter abnormal, and no other app on the owner's
259	Mac wedges the mic on sleep.
260	
261	`AudioHub.prepareFormat()` → `renewEngine()` → `makeEngine()`, and `makeEngine()`
262	touches `engine.inputNode`. **That property access opens the default input device
263	and mints a hidden per-client aggregate device inside coreaudiod**
264	(`CADefaultDeviceAggregate-<pid>-<n>`); a failed start tears it back down. So a
265	"retry" was never a format read — it was a device open plus an aggregate
266	create/destroy. One measured outage ran that cycle **~210 times over 3h40m**,
267	against hardware that was not there at all.
268	
269	Two independent things say that is the wrong shape:
270	
271	- **The information was already free.** `AudioDiagnostics` reads
272	  `kAudioHardwarePropertyDevices` and the per-device properties every five
273	  seconds, entirely with `AudioObjectGetPropertyData` property queries that open
274	  nothing. The expensive question was never buying an answer we didn't have.
275	- **The symptom shape is a known CoreAudio failure with this exact fingerprint.**
276	  `AVAudioEngine`'s hidden aggregate going stale presents as *engine running,
277	  buffers completing, no audio* — which is our no-signal state precisely, and it
278	  is documented on the output side with "only switching the device and back fixes
279	  it" (our replug). Ours had gone further than a stale aggregate, since `killall
280	  coreaudiod` did not clear it — but the failure family is the same, and we were
281	  churning the exact object at the centre of it.
282	
283	So `finishListening()` now calls `requireSettledInputDevice()` **before**
284	`prepareFormat()`, and it throws into the existing failed-start catch — so a
285	refusal reuses the whole logged/counted/retried path rather than growing a second
286	recovery mechanism beside it. Two requirements:
287	
288	- **A device the HAL says is openable**, judged by `AudioDiagnostics.hasUsableInput`:
289	  non-aggregate (counting our own aggregate would report a usable input *because*
290	  we already opened one), alive, and with a **nonzero rate and sane channel
291	  count** — mere presence is the `outputFormat` trap one layer down.
292	- **Continuously present for `deviceSettleDelay` (6s)**, which is longer than the
293	  5s sample interval, so the gate can never be satisfied by the same observation
294	  that first revealed the device. The wedge episode opened the mic *in the same
295	  second it appeared* — via the config-change handler, not the ladder, which is
296	  why the gate belongs at `finishListening` where both paths meet.
297	
298	Effect on the measured outage: **~210 device opens → 0.** Nothing is opened until
299	there is something to open.
300	
301	**What is proven and what is not.** Proven: the churn was real, was
302	under-costed by its own comment, and is unlike any ordinary audio app. *Not*
303	proven: that it caused the wedge. The mic reported a sane `48000Hz/2ch/alive=y`
304	when we grabbed it, which is evidence against the mid-enumeration story
305	specifically. Treat this as removing the only mechanism by which we could
306	plausibly damage a device — not as a confirmed root-cause fix. **If it recurs,
307	that is information, not a reason to assume the gate failed.**
308	
309	### A settle gate applies to arrivals you *witnessed*, not to what was already there
310	
311	The gate above shipped in 0.5.0 with a bug that made the app look broken on every
312	launch: it refused to start listening for ~19 seconds, which reads as "it doesn't
313	start" and sent the owner to the menu to switch it on by hand.
314	
315	Two things compounded:
316	
317	- **`Timer(timeInterval:repeats:)` does not fire immediately.** The first sample
318	  lands one `sampleInterval` (5s) *after* `AudioDiagnostics.start()`, and
319	  `usableInputSince` was only ever set inside `sample()` — so for the app's first
320	  five seconds the probe reported "no input device" about a microphone sitting
321	  right there. Any state a timer maintains needs **seeding at start**, not just
322	  updating on tick.
323	- **Then the settle clock started from first observation**, costing another 6s,
324	  and the retry ladder's 2→4→8s backoff pushed the first viable attempt to ~19s.
325	
326	The conceptual error is the second one, and it is the reusable lesson: *"it
327	appeared N seconds ago" is a claim you can only make about a transition you
328	watched happen.* A device that was already present when sampling began has been
329	there for as long as the Mac has been up; there is no enumeration race to lose,
330	and waiting is pure cost. So `usableInputFor` reports `.greatestFiniteMagnitude`
331	for a device found already present (`witnessedArrival == false`), and a real
332	duration only for one seen to arrive — which is exactly the wedge case the gate
333	exists for, and still gets its full settle window.
334	
335	### A continuity claim cannot span a gap in observation — and sleep is one (#107)
336	
337	The wedge recurred on 0.5.0, after a sleep, **with the settle gate in place and
338	doing nothing**: menu bar on ⚠️ *no signal*, and System Settings → Sound → Input
339	showing a dead meter, the same system-wide shape as #88.
340	
341	The gate was a no-op on the wake path, in both 0.5.0 and the 0.5.1 refinement
342	above, for one reason: `usableInputSince` was carried straight *through* the
343	sleep. `AudioDiagnostics`' sampling timer does not fire while the machine is
344	asleep, so a mic that powered down, re-enumerated and came back was still
345	reported as having been continuously present since before the sleep — in 0.5.0 as
346	a long elapsed run, in 0.5.1 as `.greatestFiniteMagnitude` via
347	`witnessedArrival == false`. Either way `requireSettledInputDevice()` passed
348	instantly and the resume opened the device with **zero** settle: precisely the
349	"opened it in the same second it appeared" hazard the gate was added to stop, on
350	precisely the transition it was built for.
351	
352	The reusable shape, and the one to check against any future "it has been X for N
353	seconds" state: **a duration is a claim about a span you observed, so it is only
354	as good as the observation behind it.** The previous section established that
355	"already present when we started watching" needs no settle window; the missing
356	half is that the clause only holds *while you are still watching*. A blind spot
357	inside the run invalidates the whole run, because what the run asserts —
358	"nothing happened to this device" — is exactly what a blind spot cannot support.
359	
360	So `AudioDiagnostics` tracks observation as its own state:
361	
362	- **`inputAvailability` is a three-state enum, not a duration-or-nil.**
363	  `.absent` ("no default input device worth opening") and `.unobserved` ("we have
364	  not been watching") are different answers and only one of them is about the
365	  hardware. Collapsing them would have put an unmeasured claim about the mic into
366	  the log — the sin #79 and #88 were both about.
367	- **`noteObservationInterrupted()` is called from `willSleep`**, so a sleep is
368	  *declared* rather than inferred. Inferring it from elapsed time misses a sleep
369	  shorter than the tolerance, and the USB bus is powered down for a short sleep
370	  too. The elapsed-time backstop in `sample()` stays for interruptions nobody
371	  announces — and it must measure with **`Date()`, not `systemUptime`**, the one
372	  place in this file that inverts the usual rule: the span being measured is the
373	  span the monotonic clock refuses to count.
374	- **The run is keyed on the device's UID**, not on "is anything usable?". A mic
375	  swapped for another between two samples is a new arrival that has settled for
376	  zero seconds, and a set-level predicate cannot see that happen at all.
377	- **`usableInput()` judges the *system default* input**, which is the device
378	  `AVAudioEngine` actually opens — a healthy mic behind a broken default is not a
379	  mic we can capture from. That also subsumes the old exclude-aggregates rule
380	  (our hidden `CADefaultDeviceAggregate` is never the system default) and fixes
381	  its collateral damage: a user's deliberately-built aggregate device is a fine
382	  thing to capture from, and the old predicate refused it.
383	
384	**Still unproven, and still the whole question:** that opening a device
385	mid-enumeration is what wedges it. This recurrence is *consistent* with the
386	theory — the gate meant to prevent it was inert across sleep, which is when the
387	wedge keeps happening — but consistency is not proof, and the same recurrence is
388	equally consistent with the gate being irrelevant. What it does settle is
389	narrower and worth keeping separate: **the mitigation shipped in 0.5.0 was never
390	actually exercised on the wake path**, so 0.5.0 recurring says nothing about
391	whether the mitigation works. The next recurrence is the first one that will.
392	
393	## Diagnostics must not assume a toolchain on the owner's Mac
394	
395	The Mac running LaughCounter installs the DMG from CI and has **no Xcode command
396	line tools** — so anything needed to diagnose a live failure has to be either
397	shell built into macOS, or compiled into the app by CI. That is why the HAL reads
398	live in the app rather than in a helper script.
399	
400	`command -v swift` does **not** test for a Swift toolchain: `/usr/bin/swift`
401	ships on every Mac as a stub that pops the *"install the command line developer
402	tools?"* dialog when run, so the check passes and the script prompts the owner to
403	install 8 GB of Xcode. Gate on `xcode-select -p >/dev/null 2>&1` first — it fails
404	quietly when the tools are absent.
405	
406	## Exit paths: `applicationWillTerminate` is not "every exit path" by itself
407	
408	`NSApp.terminate` (menu Quit, ⌘Q, the logout/shutdown quit Apple Event) runs
409	`applicationWillTerminate` — but **NSApplication installs no signal handlers**:
410	a bare SIGTERM (Activity Monitor "Quit", `killall`), SIGINT (Ctrl-C in a dev
411	terminal), or SIGHUP kills the process with no teardown. `main.swift` routes
412	those through `DispatchSourceSignal` → `NSApp.terminate`; the `signal(sig,
413	SIG_IGN)` must precede `resume()` or a signal in the gap still takes the fatal
414	default. SIGKILL/Force-Quit/crash remain uncoverable — residual risk, not a bug.
415	Don't add `NSSupportsSuddenTermination` to Info.plist: it would let logout
416	SIGKILL the app past all of this.
417	
418	## Deferred work must be generation-guarded
419	
420	`asyncAfter` timers scheduled before sleep **fire immediately on wake** — so any
421	delayed engine start (the +0.4s `finishListening`, the +1.0s wake resume) that a
422	stop raced with would otherwise re-acquire the mic going *into* sleep or
423	un-settled at wake. Every intentional stop bumps `restartGeneration`; every
424	delayed closure captures the generation at schedule time and aborts if it moved.
425	When cancelling in-flight restarts, also reset `restartInFlight` /
426	`restartQueued` / `suppressConfigChange`, or the latches stay stuck and block
427	all future starts.
428	
429	## There is no "returned from standby" notification — fan in, then coalesce
430	
431	macOS distinguishes sleep depths internally but exposes no standby-specific event:
432	`NSWorkspace.didWakeNotification` is all you get, and it is **not equivalent to "the
433	machine is back"** — a dark/Power-Nap wake fires it with nobody there and the Mac
434	re-sleeps moments later. So `systemDidReturn(reason:)` fans in four signals —
435	`didWake`, `screensDidWake`, `sessionDidBecomeActive`, and the distributed
436	`com.apple.screenIsUnlocked` — and coalesces them, because a real return fires
437	several of them in a burst and each must not schedule its own restart:
438	
439	- **Coalesce with an id, not a bool.** `pendingResumeID` holds the one in-flight
440	  resume; a stale timer compares its captured id and returns without touching
441	  state. A bare `resumePending` bool deadlocks: a re-sleep during the delay
442	  invalidates the timer, the timer clears the bool, and whichever of the two
443	  orderings loses leaves the next wake either unable to schedule (flag stuck true)
444	  or double-scheduling.
445	- **Gate on owing a resume**, i.e. `sleeping || (listeningIntent && !listening)`.
446	  Displays wake and sessions activate with no sleep involved (screensaver, user
447	  switching); reacting to those would cycle a healthy engine — the wedge condition.
448	- **Always ungate `sleeping` in the resume timer**, even on the "stay off" path, or
449	  `requestListening` stays blocked forever and the menu's Start item does nothing.
450	- The distributed unlock notification is free here because the app is
451	  non–App Store (no App Sandbox). Under the sandbox it silently never arrives; the
452	  three workspace triggers still cover the case.
453	
454	## Resume by *intent*, and retry — a failed post-standby start has no second event
455	
456	`listening` ("the engine is running") is not the state a wake should branch on.
457	`listeningIntent` ("the counter is meant to be running") is: sleep suspends capture
458	without clearing it, so a return reactivates only a counter that was actually
459	active, while a start that merely *failed* keeps it and stays eligible for recovery.
460	Branching on `listening` instead would make any pre-sleep failure permanent.
461	
462	The intent is stored as `offReason: String?` — nil means "meant to be running" and
463	`listeningIntent` is derived from it — rather than a bool beside a separate reason
464	string. The menu status, the tooltip and the wake log all render that one field, so
465	they cannot disagree about whether the counter is off or why ("paused",
466	"no microphone access", "starting up"). Menu **Pause listening** sets it; every
467	request to listen clears it, which is what asking to listen means.
468	
469	After a long standby the USB bus was powered down and the mic can still be
470	re-enumerating when the settle window closes. That start throws, and — unlike the
471	config-change cases — **nothing else will ever fire** to recover from it, so the app
472	sits silently "not listening" until someone opens the menu. Hence
473	`scheduleStartRetry`: doubling 2s → 32s, capped at `maxStartRetries`, reset on every
474	success / system return / manual resume. Bounded on purpose (a mic that is gone for
475	good emits nothing and must not be polled forever) and slow on purpose (rapid-cycling
476	is what wedges the mic). The wake settle is also stretched 1.0s → 2.5s when the sleep
477	lasted longer than `standbyThreshold`; measure that span with `Date()`, **not**
478	`ProcessInfo.systemUptime`, which does not advance while the machine is asleep.
479	
480	## Config-change suppression must reconcile, not just drop
481	
482	CoreAudio posts `.AVAudioEngineConfigurationChange` for our *own* stop/start
483	(react → infinite restart loop, hence the suppress window) **and** for genuine
484	device events — including while the machine heads into sleep (hence the
485	`sleeping` gate from `willSleep` until the post-wake settle). A genuine event
486	swallowed by the window is reconciled at settle time by *state*, not by the
487	notification: engine dead while `listening` → restart; start failed and an
488	event arrived → one retry per swallowed event (a dead mic emits no events, so
489	this can't poll).
490	
491	## Misc gotchas that bit
492	
493	- `engine.stop()` unconditionally in `AudioHub.stop()`: it's safe when not
494	  running and it releases what `prepare()` allocated — a prepare-then-throw
495	  path would otherwise keep the input unit holding the device.
496	- `installTap` with a format the hardware no longer matches raises an
497	  **uncatchable NSException** — re-validate the live format immediately before
498	  the tap (narrows, doesn't eliminate; there is no atomic API).
499	- `SFSpeechRecognizer` fed via `SFSpeechAudioBufferRecognitionRequest` never
500	  holds the device — it can't cause the wedge. But its state is touched from
501	  main, the Speech callback queue, *and* the audio tap thread: everything in
502	  `VoiceCommand` goes through one lock, and the two-phase `start()` gates the
503	  task store on *request identity* (`request === newRequest`), because a
504	  restart() between the phases leaves `running == true` — gating on `running`
505	  would store a dead task and permanently block the idempotency guard.
506

1	# Evaluating and routing a new item
2	
3	The shared method for three decisions every proposed addition to this corpus must pass through: **is it worthy** of inclusion at all, **which mechanism** should carry it, and — only for prose — **where does it go**. Any routine or person that adds an item — the [growth promote stage](tasks/growth-promote/task.md), an owner-requested retrospective pass, a hand edit — applies this same protocol, so the decision-making lives here once instead of being re-derived per caller.
4	
5	This is a Claudinite-internal doc used by the growth lifecycle (see [the canon-curation README](README.md)): it is **not** part of the mounted corpus and consuming repos do not `@import` it.
6	
7	An "item" is one **distilled, portable rule** — not a transcript, not a narration of what happened. A candidate still phrased as "here's what we did" has not been distilled yet and is below the bar on form alone, before any of the tests below. This doc picks up once a distilled rule exists and decides its fate.
8	
9	## Worthiness — does it earn a place at all
10	
11	The corpus is read read-only by every consuming repo, so a **duplicative** item (already covered) or an **undistilled** one (a story or a truism, not a rule) pollutes shared canon and costs every future reader. The bar guards against *those* — it is **not** a bar on *scope*: an item useful to only one project today can still earn a place (see Portable). Admit an item only when **all** hold:
12	
13	- **Distilled.** It is a single tight rule in the imperative, not a story, a log, or a restatement of a generic truism.
14	- **Portable — would a *future* project benefit?** Not "useful to every project today." An item can help only **one** project right now and still belong here, so long as another project — **especially one with a similar tech stack or process** — would benefit when it arrives. Being specific to a technology or a process is **not** disqualifying: generalize it and route it to that technology's or practice's home. What disqualifies is leaning on *this* project's non-transferable particulars — a product requirement, or a one-off incident in how it happened to call some API. The test, a genuinely hard one: *if another project with a similar tech stack came along, would it benefit from this?* Yes → portable; only-ever-this-product → local. A rule mined from Claudinite's own test suite is the hardest case: it reads as generic testing craft even when it actually depends on Claudinite's own shape — the only project whose tests build git-repo fixtures because its checks take a repo as input. Before promoting one, grep the fleet's own callers of the pattern the rule is about; zero callers outside this project's own conformance tests means the lesson is local however general its wording (#857: a fixture-signing rule read as portable, was promoted to `writing-tests`, then reverted once every caller of the fixture helper turned out to be a Claudinite conformance test).
15	- **Durable and reusable.** It will still apply on a future, unseen task — not a one-off, not a situational detail, not something already implied by an existing rule.
16	- **Readable through the channel it lands in.** A rule whose premise is that the delivery channel
17	  itself failed cannot be carried by that channel. Promote #497 admitted "the tell that the SessionStart
18	  hook did not fire" as pack prose — and pack prose is what that hook delivers, so in the one situation
19	  the rule describes it is not in context to be read. Detecting a channel's own failure belongs in code,
20	  not in the payload the channel carries; reject such an item here rather than rewording it.
21	- **Not already covered.** The insight does not already exist **anywhere** in the corpus, even worded differently or owned by a different file. This is checked against the *entire* corpus, not just the file it would land in — see [Dedupe against the whole corpus](#dedupe-against-the-whole-corpus).
22	
23	Reject on any miss — but the misses that matter are *undistilled*, *already-covered*, or *genuinely one-off*, not merely *narrow*. When you're torn over a real, non-duplicate rule, lean toward **keeping** it — the goal is a broad library. When you're torn over whether something is a duplicate, or a rule at all, leave it out. The failure to avoid is padding the canon with restatements of what's already there; admitting a narrow-but-reusable rule is not that failure.
24	
25	### Dedupe against the whole corpus
26	
27	Before admitting anything, read across the corpus, not only the file you expect to own the item. The same insight is frequently already present under a different heading or in an adjacent group. If it sharpens an **existing** rule, fold it in with a minimal edit rather than adding a second bullet that says nearly the same thing — and never weaken or restate what is already there in the process.
28	
29	**Sweep last, and case-insensitively.** A dedupe pass is only evidence about the text it actually read, so it runs **after** every re-home, merge and edit the change makes — a sweep run early and never re-run reports clean on content that has since moved under it. Measured on #740 (the seven-PR promote consolidation): the sweep ran *before* two lessons were re-homed out of a folded-away skill file into `packs/basics/RULES.md`, and **three** copies of the same unknown-state rule reached the owner, who found them by reading. The re-run then surfaced a further pair the pattern had missed because it was case-sensitive and the survivors were capitalised. So: sweep as the last step, match case-insensitively, and state the similarity threshold you swept at so the "no remaining near-duplicates" claim is checkable.
30	
31	## Mechanism triage — prose is the fallback, not the default
32	
33	A worthy item next descends the **promotion ladder** ([../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md) owns it): platform setting (always paired with its verifying check) → PreToolUse hook → conformance check → skill → prose. The *first* rung that can carry the item wins — a rule about repo state becomes a check whose failure message *is* the lesson; a bad action to prevent becomes a guard; a procedure or knowledge with a nameable trigger becomes (or joins) a skill. Only an item none of those can carry — judgment, in-flight behavior, signature-less knowledge — proceeds to the file routing below, and its landing **names that reason** in the promote log so conversion rates stay auditable.
34	
35	**"No universal signature" alone never routes an item to prose.** A rule converts to a check when a *narrow, file-scoped* signature covers the **grounded cases** — the concrete shapes the rule was distilled from — even though no signature covers every conceivable violation. Gate it relevance-first so it stays inert off-target, and document the genuinely signature-less residue in the rule's own comments as out of scope. The prose rung is only for an item whose grounded cases *themselves* have no reliable signature (pure judgment, runtime/in-flight behavior).
36	
37	## Routing — picking the right file (rung-5 items only)
38	
39	Routing is robust when it keys on **stable file groups**, not on the current roster of individual files (which grows over time). The corpus is organized into a few groups, each with its own selection rule:
40	
41	1. **The practice group** — durable, project-agnostic practices, each file a self-contained, reusable unit of know-how the agent applies whenever its subject comes up (engineering, agentic, git/GitHub, testing, investigation, discipline, architecture), partitioned **by kind of practice** with each file owning one recurring subject cluster. This group spans **two folders that differ only by *when* the rule loads**: `always/` for a rule that applies to essentially every task (the index `@`-imports it, so it's force-loaded every session), and `tasks/` for a subject-gated rule read on demand when its trigger fires. Route in two steps: first match the item's *kind* to the file whose cluster already owns that subject; then keep it in `always/` only if it genuinely isn't tied to one kind of task (the rare case — `always/` stays small), otherwise it belongs in `tasks/`. Read the group's own index (the root `CLAUDE.md`) to find the current owner for a kind — never from memory, since the set of clusters can grow.
42	2. **The per-user group** — interaction preferences and trigger phrases. This group does **not live in this repo**: an item of this kind routes out to the person it belongs to, never into the practice group and never back into the canon.
43	3. **The per-technology group** — practices specific to one technology, **one file per technology**. Route a technology-specific item to that technology's file. When **no pack homes that technology** (not even a stub), the item doesn't land in a loose doc — it **mints a fingerprinted stub pack** (a `packs/<tech>/`, delivered in its own PR), so the next project on that stack self-declares it; [promote](tasks/growth-promote/task.md)'s stub-minting floor and [the generate-project-instructions skill](../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/skills/generate-project-instructions/SKILL.md) own the mechanics.
44	
45	Pick **exactly one** owner. If an item plausibly fits two files, choose the single best one — never split one item across files, and never duplicate it into both. The group decides the *axis* (kind, person, or technology); the file within the group is then the one whose existing scope the item falls squarely inside.
46	
47	### When nothing fits
48	
49	An item that matches **no** existing file is **not** a reject signal by itself — a genuinely new category of lesson is meant to be learnable, so a worthy item that no file owns earns its own file. Resolve it in this order:
50	
51	- **Route into an existing owner** when one genuinely fits — the first choice. If the item belongs to a file's cluster and merely sits slightly off-center, a small stretch toward that owner beats spinning up a new file. A new file is for when no existing file's scope genuinely fits, **not** a way to dodge folding into an existing owner.
52	- **Open a new file** when the item clears the [Worthiness](#worthiness--does-it-earn-a-place-at-all) bar in full — distilled, portable, durable and reusable, and not already covered anywhere in the corpus — **and** no existing file's scope genuinely fits it. That is the whole bar: nothing more is required. Do **not** also demand that you expect the cluster to recur, that forcing the item into the closest file would *distort* it, or default to rejecting when the new-file call is a close one — those extra hurdles are dropped. Creating a file obliges registering it where the corpus is indexed and in any routing table, in the **same** change, so it never lands orphaned (see [Keep the write surface bounded](#keep-the-write-surface-bounded)).
53	
54	The loosening above is **only** to the new-cluster hurdle, never to the per-item bar. An item that misses [Worthiness](#worthiness--does-it-earn-a-place-at-all) — a one-off, non-portable or project-specific, a restatement of a generic truism, or already covered anywhere in the corpus — is rejected whether or not a file already exists for it; for the per-item admission decision, the default-to-reject-when-unsure tiebreak still stands.
55	
56	## Keep the write surface bounded
57	
58	Once worthiness and routing are settled, the edit touches **only** the single owning file: add or sharpen one terse rule in that file's existing voice and format, and change nothing else. Do not "improve" unrelated rules while you are in there. The sole exception is the new-file path above, whose surface is itself bounded to the new file plus its index and routing-table registration.
59
